lessons.description: Targeted review of scientific notation and electronic prefix conversions, grounded in Chapter 3, “Math for Electronics,” by Fitz Herbert Reid, CET, printed pp. 16–17. These topics already appear in Mathematics Companion; this review adds a unit-ratio method and conversion checks using the chapter’s verified examples.

review_lessons.title: Prefix Conversions by Unit Ratios and Reverse Checks

sections.body: This is reinforcement of the powers-of-ten and metric-prefix material already covered in Mathematics Companion, not a new circuit concept. The source-specific contribution is the chapter’s notation examples and electronic conversions: printed p. 16 gives 125000 = 1.25 × 10^5, 0.125 = 1.25 × 10^-1, and 0.007 = 7 × 10^-3; its conversion examples continue onto printed p. 17. The alternative method here is instructional: express the starting unit as a power of ten, divide by the size of the target unit, and check the direction of the numerical change. All practice questions below are newly authored, not transcribed book exercises.
sections.heading: Review purpose and source contribution

sections.body: Scientific notation separates a number into a coefficient and a scale factor. In 1.25 × 10^5, the factor 10^5 means 100000, so multiplication recovers 125000. A negative exponent denotes a reciprocal: 10^-3 = 1/1000. Thus the source’s 0.007 = 7 × 10^-3 means seven thousandths, not a negative number. For standard scientific notation of a positive value, use a coefficient at least 1 and less than 10. When rewriting the number, preserve its value: if the coefficient becomes ten times smaller, the power-of-ten factor must become ten times larger. Check by multiplying the coefficient by the scale factor rather than trusting a remembered decimal-shift direction.
sections.heading: Recover the value from the exponent

sections.body: The prefix table on printed p. 16 identifies pico as 10^-12 and micro as 10^-6. Here F abbreviates farad, so pF and µF name different-sized units of capacitance. For the verified example, first write 1000 pF = 1000 × 10^-12 F = 10^-9 F. One microfarad is 10^-6 F; therefore the numerical value in microfarads is 10^-9/10^-6 = 10^-3. This gives 1000 pF = 0.001 µF, matching the source. Equivalently, multiply 1000 pF by the unit ratio (1 µF)/(1000000 pF); the pF units cancel. That ratio equals one, so it changes the unit expression without changing the capacitance. The result should have a smaller numerical value because µF is the larger unit.
sections.heading: Worked source example: picofarads to microfarads

sections.body: The verified frequency example on printed pp. 16–17 is 700 kHz = 700000 Hz = 0.7 MHz. Hz abbreviates hertz; k means kilo, or 10^3, and M means mega, or 10^6. Starting in hertz makes both steps visible: 700 kHz = 700 × 10^3 Hz = 7 × 10^5 Hz. To express this in megahertz, divide its hertz value by 10^6: (7 × 10^5)/(10^6) = 7 × 10^-1 = 0.7 MHz. Preserve prefix case: the source’s kilo and mega prefixes are written k and M. Finally, reverse the conversion: 0.7 MHz × 1000 kHz/MHz = 700 kHz. The unchanged starting value is a useful arithmetic check; the magnitude check is that larger units give smaller numerical values.
sections.heading: Worked source example: one frequency, three unit expressions

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Write 470000 and 0.000032 in scientific notation. Show how the power of ten preserves each original value.
questions.explanation: 470000 = 4.7 × 100000 = 4.7 × 10^5. Also, 0.000032 = 3.2 × 0.00001 = 3.2 × 10^-5. In each case the coefficient lies between 1 and 10. The exponent records the scale, rather than changing the number.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Convert 2200 pF to µF using an intermediate value in farads.
questions.explanation: Pico means 10^-12 and micro means 10^-6. Thus 2200 pF = 2200 × 10^-12 F = 2.2 × 10^-9 F. Expressing that value in microfarads gives (2.2 × 10^-9)/(10^-6) = 2.2 × 10^-3 µF. The numerical value becomes smaller because a microfarad is a larger unit than a picofarad.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Convert 450 kHz to both Hz and MHz. Explain why one numerical result is larger than 450 and the other is smaller.
questions.explanation: A kilohertz is 1000 hertz, so 450 kHz = 450 × 1000 Hz = 450000 Hz. A megahertz is 1000 kilohertz, so 450 kHz = 450/1000 MHz = 0.45 MHz. Smaller units require more units to describe the same frequency; larger units require fewer.

questions.answer: The conversion should divide by 10^6: 680 pF = 0.000680 µF.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A calculation claims that 680 pF = 680000000 µF. Identify the direction error and give the correct conversion.
questions.explanation: Going from picofarads to microfarads means expressing the same capacitance in a unit one million times larger. Divide the numerical value by one million, rather than multiply: 680/1000000 = 0.000680. A reverse check gives 0.000680 × 1000000 = 680 pF.

questions.answer: 0.125 MHz = 125 kHz = 125000 Hz; reversing the conversion returns 0.125 MHz.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Convert 0.125 MHz to kHz and then Hz. Use a reverse conversion to check your answer, and preserve the prefix capitalization.
questions.explanation: Mega represents 10^6 and kilo represents 10^3. Therefore 0.125 MHz = 0.125 × 1000 kHz = 125 kHz, and 125 kHz = 125 × 1000 Hz = 125000 Hz. Reversing the calculation, 125000 Hz divided by 10^6 gives 0.125 MHz. Write lowercase k for kilo and uppercase M for mega.

review_lessons.new_perspective: Instead of relying on decimal shifts, convert through the base unit or multiply by a unit ratio equal to one. Use both a larger-unit/smaller-number check and a reverse conversion. The book-specific reinforcement is its verified scientific-notation, pF-to-µF, and kHz-to-Hz/MHz examples; the checking method and fresh exercises are instructional additions.

review_lessons.title: Rearrange, Then Test the Original Equality

sections.body: The verified “Equations” material on printed p. 17 describes an equation as an equality and uses letters for numerical quantities or unknowns. Its examples include a = bc, b = a/c, c = a/b, and 4y = 2. These are the source-specific anchors for this review. Equation rearrangement is a listed topic of Mathematics Companion; this connection does not establish that you have completed it. The alternative approach here pairs each rearrangement with a substitution check. The explanations and fresh practice are instructional additions, not additional transcribed book examples.
sections.heading: Source anchors and review approach

sections.body: An equals sign says that the expressions on its two sides have the same value. A letter names a quantity; its value may be given or may be the unknown you want to find. In a = bc, the adjacent letters bc mean b multiplied by c. The equation therefore says that a equals the product of b and c. Rearranging does not change this relationship: it expresses the same relationship with a different letter isolated. These examples supply no physical units, so treat the letters as numerical quantities rather than assigning them electrical meanings.
sections.heading: Read the relationship before calculating

sections.body: The source example 4y = 2 means four times y equals two. To leave y by itself, undo multiplication by 4 with division by 4. Apply that operation to both sides: (4y)/4 = 2/4. Since 4/4 = 1, the left side becomes y, giving y = 2/4 = 0.5. The fraction 2/4 means two divided by four; it can also be simplified to 1/2. Now check the result in the original equation: 4 × 0.5 = 2. This check tests the answer against the starting relationship, rather than merely repeating the division.
sections.heading: Worked source example: solve and substitute

sections.body: For a = bc, choose which letter you want alone. To isolate b, undo its multiplication by c: divide both sides by c to obtain a/c = bc/c = b, or b = a/c. This step requires c ≠ 0. To isolate c instead, divide both sides by b: a/b = bc/b = c, or c = a/b, with b ≠ 0. Both quotient forms appear in the verified source; the nonzero conditions are mathematical qualifications explained here. Choose the divisor by identifying the factor multiplying your desired unknown, not by guessing which letter should go above the fraction bar.
sections.heading: Rearrange a product into a quotient

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Solve 4y = 2. Explain which operation preserves equality, then check your answer in the original equation.
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 4: y = 2/4 = 0.5. Substituting gives 4 × 0.5 = 2, so the original equality holds. The fraction 2/4 and the decimal 0.5 describe the same value.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Solve 6x = 3 and verify the result by multiplication.
questions.explanation: The coefficient 6 multiplies x, so divide both sides by 6: x = 3/6 = 1/2 = 0.5. The check is 6 × 0.5 = 3.

questions.answer: b = a/c; for the supplied values, b = 6.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Starting with a = bc, isolate b. Then find b when a = 18 and c = 3.
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by c, assuming c is not zero: a/c = bc/c = b. Substitution gives b = 18/3 = 6. Check the original product: 6 × 3 = 18.

questions.answer: c = a/b; for the supplied values, c = 3.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Starting with a = bc, isolate c. Then find c when a = 7.5 and b = 2.5.
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by the nonzero factor b: c = a/b. With the supplied values, c = 7.5/2.5 = 3. Checking gives 2.5 × 3 = 7.5.

questions.answer: The proposed rearrangement fails. The correct expression is b = a/c, giving b = 3.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A learner changes a = bc into b = c/a. Test that proposed rearrangement using a = 12 and c = 4, and give the correct rearrangement.
questions.explanation: The proposed expression gives b = 4/12 = 1/3. Substitution into the original equation gives bc = (1/3) × 4 = 4/3, not 12. Dividing the original equation by c instead gives b = a/c = 12/4 = 3, and 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.answer: No. Division by zero is undefined, and the original equation does not determine a unique value of b.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: In a = bc, suppose a = 0 and c = 0. Can b be found by dividing a by c? What does the original equation tell you?
questions.explanation: The quotient a/c would be 0/0, which is undefined. Returning to the original equation gives 0 = b × 0. That equality holds for every numerical value of b, so these given values do not determine a unique b.

review_lessons.new_perspective: Use the original equation as an independent test of every rearrangement: identify the multiplication, undo it on both sides, and substitute the result back. The source-specific contribution is the p. 17 product-and-quotient examples and 4y = 2; the substitution workflow, explicit nonzero-divisor qualifications, and error-detection exercises provide targeted reinforcement rather than a new source concept.

plan.goal: Distinguish a formula variable from a unit abbreviation and interpret the chapter’s electronic and Greek notation.
plan.focus: Use the units and Greek-letter tables as reference tools. Distinguish resistance, reactance and impedance from their shared ohm unit; recognize siemens entries without expanding into unseen admittance theory. Define context-dependent symbols locally, including capacitance versus coulombs and voltage versus energy notation.
plan.title: Reading Formula Symbols and Units

lessons.title: Reading Formula Symbols and Units

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
A formula symbol represents a quantity; a unit abbreviation tells you how a value of that quantity is expressed. These are different roles, even when the same letter appears in both. The “Units for Electronics Formulas” table on printed p. 24 explicitly distinguishes formula symbols from unit abbreviations.

A useful reading method is to ask three questions: What quantity does this symbol represent here? What unit measures it? What numerical value is being supplied? Do not decide the meaning from the letter alone. Read the accompanying definition and the equation in which it appears.

This lesson uses the table as a reference tool, not a list to memorize. The verified extraction supports selected distinctions, rather than a complete transcription of every table entry. Where an individual entry is not supplied, we will not reconstruct it.
sections.heading: Separate the quantity from its unit

sections.body:
Printed p. 24 groups resistance, reactance and impedance under the same unit: ohms. This is a shared measurement unit, not a statement that the three quantity names mean the same thing. For example, a value identified as “5 ohms of resistance” and one identified as “5 ohms of impedance” have the same numerical value and unit, but their quantity labels remain different. This is a newly authored notation example, not a circuit calculation from the book.

The table also assigns siemens to conductance, admittance and susceptance. At this stage, recognize those three names and their shared unit; the supplied table evidence does not establish how to calculate them or how they behave in a circuit.

When reading a result, retain both the quantity label and its unit. A unit can help classify a value, but it does not always identify the quantity uniquely. This is why a clear answer needs more than an unexplained number followed by a unit.
sections.heading: Shared units do not make quantities identical

sections.body:
The period-and-frequency material on printed p. 19 uses T for period and f for frequency; the source also uses capital F for frequency. Period is measured in seconds and frequency in hertz. Thus, in T = 1/f, the letters name quantities, while “seconds” and “hertz” name their units. This is a notation reading, not a requirement to perform reciprocal calculations before continuing.

Printed p. 20 supplies another important distinction: C represents capacitance in Q = CV, but the unit of charge is the coulomb, abbreviated C. Here Q is charge in coulombs, C is capacitance in farads, and V is voltage in volts. The same character can therefore serve different roles according to its position and definition. Likewise, F may represent frequency in the source’s formula notation, whereas F as a unit abbreviation means farad.

Read the locally defined meaning first. A symbol in an equation and a unit after a numerical value should not automatically receive the same interpretation.
sections.heading: Read T, f, F and C in context

sections.body:
The clear energy definition on printed p. 20 is E = 0.5CV². In this equation, E means stored electric-field energy in joules, C means capacitance in farads, and V means voltage in volts. The squared symbol is V: the expression uses voltage multiplied by itself. This reading identifies the symbols without developing the separate lesson on capacitor energy calculations.

The extraction flags conflicting notation in the right-column energy solution, where E is used both as an energy label and inside an expression. That ambiguity remains unresolved. Use the clear definition above for this notation exercise; do not guess the meaning of every E in the disputed solution or silently repair it.

Printed p. 24 also contains a table pairing Greek uppercase and lowercase letters with their names. Use such a table to identify a character and its case, then use the surrounding formula definition to determine what quantity it represents. The verified extraction does not list the individual Greek entries, so this lesson does not reproduce or test unseen entries.
sections.heading: Local definitions and reference-table limits

questions.answer: Quantity: impedance. Numerical value: 5. Unit: ohm. No—the unit alone does not establish that the quantity is resistance.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A result is labeled “impedance: 5 ohms.” Identify the quantity, numerical value and unit. Does its unit alone establish that it is resistance?
questions.explanation: The p. 24 table assigns ohms to resistance, reactance and impedance. The quantity label therefore matters: sharing a unit does not make the quantities interchangeable.

questions.answer: Their shared unit is the siemens. No—the cited table entry identifies the unit, not a calculation method.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Which shared unit does the chapter assign to conductance, admittance and susceptance? Does this table entry supply a calculation method for those quantities?
questions.explanation: The verified table supports recognizing the quantity names and their unit. It does not, by itself, provide the theory or equations needed to calculate them.

questions.answer: T represents period, measured in seconds. f represents frequency, measured in hertz. A capital F defined there as frequency also represents a quantity measured in hertz; it is not automatically the farad unit.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Read T = 1/f as notation. What do T and f represent, and what units belong to each? How should you interpret a capital F if it appears as the source’s frequency symbol?
questions.explanation: The p. 19 material defines period and frequency as reciprocal quantities and also uses capital F for frequency. A locally defined formula symbol must be distinguished from a unit abbreviation such as F for farad.

questions.answer: Q is charge in coulombs, C is capacitance in farads, and V is voltage in volts. C inside this equation is a quantity symbol for capacitance; C after a numerical charge value is the unit abbreviation for coulomb.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: In Q = CV, identify each quantity and its unit. Explain the difference between C in the equation and C written as the unit abbreviation after a numerical charge value.
questions.explanation: The source defines capacitance in farads and charge in coulombs. In the formula, C names the capacitance quantity; as a unit abbreviation for charge, C means coulomb. Context resolves the repeated character.

questions.answer: E represents stored electric-field energy in joules. Voltage V is squared. No—the conflicting worked-solution notation should remain flagged rather than guessed.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: In the clear definition E = 0.5CV², what does E represent, what is its unit, and which quantity is squared? Should this definition be used to guess the meaning of every E in the source’s conflicting worked solution?
questions.explanation: The verified left-column definition uses E for energy and V for voltage. The conflicting right-column notation is unresolved, so this exercise relies only on the clear definition rather than treating an inferred correction as verified source content.

lessons.description: Targeted calculation review using the verified Ohm’s law and power material in Chapter 3, “Math for Electronics,” by Fitz Herbert Reid, CET, printed pp. 17–18. The supplied Electrical foundations lesson lists these topics; this review offers a formula-selection and cross-check method without assuming prior completion or mastery.

review_lessons.title: Select a Formula, Then Verify by Another Route

sections.body:
The source-specific anchors for this review are the Ohm’s law equations and Figure 1 on printed p. 17, followed by the readable power relations and Figures 2–3 on printed p. 18. Figure 1 places V above I and R as a memory aid; Figure 3 collects related voltage, current, resistance and power formulas. The supplied Electrical foundations lesson lists these topics, but that does not establish learner completion or mastery.

The alternative worked method here is to list the known quantities, choose an equation containing them and the desired unknown, and then check the answer through a different relation. That workflow and all numerical exercises below are newly authored reinforcement, not transcribed source problems. The extraction flags disputed power-law prose on p. 18; this review uses only the accepted equations and does not reconstruct the disputed expressions.
sections.heading: Review approach and source boundaries

sections.body:
Define the letters before selecting a formula: V is voltage in volts (V), I is current in amperes (A), R is resistance in ohms (Ω), and P is power in watts (W). Use numerical values expressed in those units for the calculations here. These are written resistor calculations, not measurement or construction instructions.

On printed p. 17, Ohm’s law gives V = IR, I = V/R and R = V/I. With current and resistance known, multiply to find voltage. With voltage and one other quantity known, divide to find the remaining quantity. The triangular memory aid can help recall this pattern, but an equation also explains it: starting from V = IR, dividing both sides by nonzero R gives V/R = I; dividing by nonzero I gives V/I = R.

Keep the requested quantity visible beside your work. V/R produces current in amperes, not power in watts. A unit label is part of the answer, not a decoration added after calculating.
sections.heading: Choose by the known quantities

sections.body:
The readable power relations on printed p. 18 are P = IV, P = I²R and P = V²/R, along with V = P/I and I = P/V. Select P = IV when current and voltage are known; P = I²R when current and resistance are known; and P = V²/R when voltage and resistance are known. The resistance-based expressions are used here for resistors, not generalized to arbitrary reactive AC loads.

These formulas connect rather than compete. Substituting V = IR into P = IV gives P = I(IR) = I²R. Substituting I = V/R gives P = (V/R)V = V²/R. This algebraic explanation is instructional reinforcement based on the verified relations.

Respect the order of operations: in I²R, square the current before multiplying by resistance; in V²/R, square the voltage before dividing. I²R does not mean (IR)². For the quotient forms, the divisor must be nonzero.
sections.heading: Link the power formulas explicitly

sections.body:
Newly authored worked example using the verified relations: a 100 Ω resistor has 5 V across it. Find its current and power. The known quantities are V = 5 V and R = 100 Ω; the unknowns are I and P.

First choose I = V/R, because it contains both given quantities: I = 5 V / 100 Ω = 0.05 A. For power, use the direct voltage-and-resistance relation: P = V²/R = (5)²/100 W = 25/100 W = 0.25 W.

Now check through a different route using the calculated current: P = IV = 0.05 × 5 W = 0.25 W. A further check gives I²R = (0.05)² × 100 W = 0.0025 × 100 W = 0.25 W. The results agree. These checks can reveal an incorrect square or a mistaken formula, although agreement alone cannot prove that the original input values were correct.
sections.heading: Worked method: calculate directly, then cross-check

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A resistor has 12 V across it and carries 0.25 A. Find its resistance and power. Check the power using a second formula.
questions.explanation: Use the two given quantities directly: R = V/I = 12/0.25 = 48 Ω, and P = IV = 0.25 × 12 = 3 W. With the calculated resistance, P = V²/R = 12²/48 = 144/48 = 3 W. Agreement supports the arithmetic and formula selection.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A 200 Ω resistor carries 0.03 A. Find its voltage and power. Show the square in the power calculation.
questions.explanation: Ohm’s law gives V = IR = 0.03 × 200 = 6 V. Because current and resistance are given, use P = I²R: (0.03)² × 200 = 0.0009 × 200 = 0.18 W. Check with P = IV = 0.03 × 6 = 0.18 W. Squaring 0.03 gives 0.0009, not 0.09.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: There is 9 V across a 300 Ω resistor. Find its current and power without using a square root.
questions.explanation: Use I = V/R = 9/300 = 0.03 A. The direct power relation for voltage and resistance is P = V²/R = 9²/300 = 81/300 = 0.27 W. Alternatively, P = IV = 0.03 × 9 = 0.27 W. No square-root rearrangement is needed.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A resistor dissipates 2 W with 10 V across it. Find its current, then its resistance.
questions.explanation: The verified power quotient is I = P/V, so I = 2/10 = 0.2 A. Then R = V/I = 10/0.2 = 50 Ω. Check with P = I²R = (0.2)² × 50 = 0.04 × 50 = 2 W.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A resistor dissipates 0.6 W while carrying 0.1 A. Find its voltage and resistance, then check the power.
questions.explanation: Use V = P/I = 0.6/0.1 = 6 V. Next, R = V/I = 6/0.1 = 60 Ω. The check is P = V²/R = 36/60 = 0.6 W. Dividing by 0.1 increases the numerical value by a factor of ten; it is not the same as multiplying by 0.1.

questions.answer: The learner calculated current and mislabeled it as power. I = 2 A; P = 16 W.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: For 8 V across a 4 Ω resistor, a learner writes P = V/R = 2 W. Identify the mistake and calculate both current and power correctly.
questions.explanation: V/R is the Ohm’s law expression for current, not power. Thus I = 8/4 = 2 A. For power, use P = V²/R = 8²/4 = 64/4 = 16 W, or P = IV = 2 × 8 = 16 W. A correct numerical division does not make the selected formula or output unit correct.

review_lessons.title: Resistor Totals: Reciprocal Stages and Magnitude Checks

sections.body:
The verified material in the lower-left column of printed p. 19 gives three calculation rules: add resistances in series, take the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals in parallel, and use R/n for equal parallel resistors. These rules are the source-specific anchors of this review; the extraction supplies no numerical worked example for this item.

The supplied lesson list includes a Series and parallel virtual laboratory. This review takes a different approach: written calculations with an intermediate-value check and a final magnitude check. It does not assume that you have completed the laboratory. All numerical examples and questions below are newly authored applications of the verified rules, not transcribed book exercises.
sections.heading: Source anchors and a calculation-focused review

sections.body:
Let R_T mean total resistance and R_1, R_2, …, R_n mean the individual resistances. Resistance is expressed here in ohms, abbreviated Ω; n is the number of resistors. Use values in the same unit before combining them. The examples assume positive resistor values and the stated series or parallel arrangement.

For series resistors, the source gives R_T = R_1 + R_2 + … + R_n. Newly authored worked example: for 100 Ω, 220 Ω and 330 Ω in series, R_T = 100 + 220 + 330 = 650 Ω. Each term is a resistance, so the sum remains in ohms.

As a check derived from this formula, adding positive resistances must give a total larger than any one of them when more than one resistor is present. A result below 330 Ω would therefore be incompatible with this example's series calculation.
sections.heading: Series: add values and inspect the sum

sections.body:
For parallel resistors, the source gives R_T = 1/(1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + … + 1/R_n). A reciprocal means one divided by a value. Calculate each reciprocal, add those results, and only then take the reciprocal of the whole sum.

Newly authored worked example: put 300 Ω and 600 Ω in parallel. First, 1/R_T = 1/300 + 1/600. Using a common denominator makes the arithmetic exact: 1/300 = 2/600, so 1/R_T = 3/600 = 1/200 Ω^-1. Now invert: R_T = 200 Ω.

The intermediate reciprocal sum has units Ω^-1, not Ω. Reporting it as the resistance would omit the final operation. For two or more positive parallel resistances, the sum of reciprocals exceeds the reciprocal of the smallest resistance. Its reciprocal must therefore be smaller than that smallest resistance. Here, 200 Ω is below 300 Ω, as expected.
sections.heading: Parallel: keep the two reciprocal stages separate

sections.body:
For n equal parallel resistors, the source supplies the shortcut R_T = R/n, where R is the resistance of each resistor. It follows directly from the general rule: adding n copies of 1/R gives n/R, and taking the reciprocal gives R/n.

Newly authored worked example: three equal 900 Ω resistors in parallel give R_T = 900/3 = 300 Ω. The full calculation agrees: 1/R_T = 1/900 + 1/900 + 1/900 = 3/900 Ω^-1, followed by R_T = 900/3 Ω.

Before using this shortcut, check that every branch resistance is equal. For unequal values, return to the reciprocal sum rather than dividing one selected resistance by the number of branches. After either method, check that the parallel total is below the smallest branch resistance. A plausible magnitude supports the calculation, but it does not replace the calculation or verify the stated connection.
sections.heading: Equal parallel resistors: derive and verify the shortcut

questions.answer: R_T = 1000 Ω, which is greater than every individual resistance.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Resistors of 120 Ω, 330 Ω and 550 Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total and give a magnitude check.
questions.explanation: Series resistances add: R_T = 120 + 330 + 550 = 1000 Ω. For these positive values, the sum is greater than the largest individual resistance, 550 Ω.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Calculate the total of 200 Ω and 300 Ω in parallel. Show the reciprocal sum before taking its reciprocal.
questions.explanation: 1/R_T = 1/200 + 1/300 = 0.005 + 0.003333… = 0.008333… Ω^-1. Taking the reciprocal gives R_T = 120 Ω. Keep enough intermediate digits to avoid unnecessary rounding error. The result is below 200 Ω, the smaller branch resistance.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Three resistors, 100 Ω, 200 Ω and 400 Ω, are connected in parallel. Find their total resistance, rounded to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The reciprocal sum is 1/100 + 1/200 + 1/400 = 0.01 + 0.005 + 0.0025 = 0.0175 Ω^-1. Therefore R_T = 1/0.0175 = 57.142857… Ω, or approximately 57.1 Ω. It is smaller than the smallest branch resistance, 100 Ω.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Four equal 680 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. Use the equal-resistor shortcut and check it with the reciprocal formula.
questions.explanation: For n equal parallel resistors, R_T = R/n = 680/4 = 170 Ω. The full formula gives 1/R_T = 4/680 Ω^-1, so R_T = 680/4 Ω again. The shortcut applies because all four resistances are equal.

questions.answer: The final reciprocal was omitted. The correct total is 50 Ω.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A learner calculates 1/100 + 1/100 = 0.02 and reports that two 100 Ω parallel resistors total 0.02 Ω. Identify the omitted step and correct the answer.
questions.explanation: The sum 0.02 has units Ω^-1 and represents 1/R_T, not R_T. Take its reciprocal: R_T = 1/0.02 = 50 Ω. The equal-resistor shortcut confirms this: 100/2 = 50 Ω.

questions.answer: Series: 300 Ω. Parallel: 75 Ω. The connection determines which total-resistance rule applies.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Compare two 150 Ω resistors connected in series with the same two values connected in parallel. Find both totals and explain why adding the values is not valid for both arrangements.
questions.explanation: Series uses direct addition: 150 + 150 = 300 Ω. Equal parallel resistors use R/n: 150/2 = 75 Ω. The source gives different rules for the two arrangements; adding branch resistances in parallel would apply the series rule to the wrong connection.

plan.goal: Explain why battery terminal voltage falls under load and calculate current using external plus internal resistance.
plan.focus: Interpret internal resistance as part of the series circuit and connect load current to internal voltage drop. Work through the verified 1.5 V and 6.25 Ω total-resistance example, then distinguish EMF from loaded terminal voltage.
plan.title: Battery EMF, Internal Resistance and Terminal Voltage

lessons.title: Battery EMF, Internal Resistance and Terminal Voltage

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Internal Resistance” material on printed p. 18, including Figure 4, models a battery as an EMF together with an internal resistance in series with the external load. EMF is the source voltage in this model, measured in volts; despite its name, electromotive force is a voltage, not a mechanical force. Internal resistance represents resistance within the source. The load is the external resistance supplied by the circuit connected to the battery.

Define the symbols locally: use EMF for source voltage, r_int for internal resistance in ohms (Ω), R_ext for external load resistance in ohms, and I for current in amperes (A). Terminal voltage, V_terminal, is the voltage available across the external load.

The important new distinction is that EMF and loaded terminal voltage need not be equal. The source explains that current produces a voltage drop across internal resistance, leaving less voltage at the terminals. This lesson develops that stated model; it does not claim that one fixed internal-resistance value completely describes every real battery.
sections.heading: Two voltages in the battery model

sections.body:
Because the internal resistance and external load are in series, include both when finding the resistance that limits current. The series rule on printed p. 19 gives R_total = R_ext + r_int. Ohm’s law on printed p. 17 then gives I = EMF/R_total, so the battery-model expression is I = EMF/(R_ext + r_int).

Use resistance values in the same unit before adding them. With EMF in volts and resistance in ohms, the calculated current is in amperes. These calculations assume a resistive load and fixed EMF and resistance values for the example.

Do not substitute EMF into I = EMF/R_ext while ignoring a specified internal resistance. That would give all of the source voltage to the load, contrary to the model. For a positive internal resistance, the denominator R_ext + r_int is larger than R_ext alone, so the calculated current is smaller. This comparison is a consequence of the verified series and Ohm’s law relations.
sections.heading: Find current from the complete series resistance

sections.body:
The verified example spanning printed pp. 18–19 uses an EMF of 1.5 V and a combined external-plus-internal resistance of 6.25 Ω. Substitute the complete resistance into the battery-model equation:

I = EMF/(R_ext + r_int)
I = 1.5 V/6.25 Ω
I = 0.24 A = 240 mA.

The last conversion expresses the same current in milliamperes: 0.24 A multiplied by 1000 mA/A is 240 mA. A substitution check gives I × R_total = 0.24 × 6.25 = 1.5 V, recovering the stated EMF.

The accepted extraction supports the combined 6.25 Ω value, but does not supply separate internal and external resistance values for this worked example. Consequently, this evidence is enough to reproduce the current, but not to calculate a separate numerical internal drop or terminal voltage. Do not invent a split of the 6.25 Ω and attribute it to the book. The next section uses explicitly newly authored values to demonstrate that additional calculation.
sections.heading: Verified source example: 1.5 V and 6.25 Ω

sections.body:
Apply Ohm’s law to each resistance in the source’s series model. The internal voltage drop is V_drop = I r_int. The remaining terminal voltage is V_terminal = EMF − I r_int. It also equals the load voltage, I R_ext. These equations express the source’s explanation of internal drop using the verified Ohm’s law relationship.

Newly authored worked example: let EMF = 3 V, r_int = 1 Ω, and R_ext = 5 Ω. First, R_total = 5 + 1 = 6 Ω. Then I = 3/6 = 0.5 A. The internal drop is 0.5 × 1 = 0.5 V, so V_terminal = 3 − 0.5 = 2.5 V. Check independently across the load: I R_ext = 0.5 × 5 = 2.5 V. Finally, 0.5 V + 2.5 V = 3 V, accounting for the source voltage.

For fixed EMF and internal resistance, a larger current produces a larger internal drop and therefore a lower terminal voltage. If current is zero, this model gives zero internal drop and terminal voltage equal to EMF. These are consequences of the model, not a practical battery-testing procedure.
sections.heading: From internal drop to loaded terminal voltage

questions.answer: Load current causes a voltage drop across the battery’s internal resistance. That internal drop accounts for the difference between EMF and loaded terminal voltage.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Explain why a battery’s terminal voltage can be lower than its EMF when it supplies a resistive load. Identify where the difference in voltage appears in the model.
questions.explanation: The internal resistance is in series with the external load. Applying Ohm’s law to that resistance gives an internal drop I r_int. The model therefore gives V_terminal = EMF − I r_int.

questions.answer: The current is 0.24 A, or 240 mA. No: the internal resistance must be known separately to calculate its voltage drop.
questions.prompt: Practice using the verified source values: A battery has an EMF of 1.5 V and a total external-plus-internal resistance of 6.25 Ω. Find the current in amperes and milliamperes. Can these values alone determine the internal voltage drop?
questions.explanation: I = 1.5/6.25 = 0.24 A = 240 mA. An internal-drop calculation requires I r_int. The combined resistance does not identify r_int separately, so the internal drop cannot be determined from these supplied values alone.

questions.answer: R_total = 12 Ω; I = 0.5 A; internal drop = 1 V; terminal voltage = 5 V. The load-voltage check also gives 5 V.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: In the stated battery model, EMF = 6 V, internal resistance = 2 Ω, and load resistance = 10 Ω. Calculate total resistance, current, internal voltage drop, and terminal voltage. Check terminal voltage using the load resistance.
questions.explanation: Add the series resistances: R_total = 10 + 2 = 12 Ω. Current is I = 6/12 = 0.5 A. The internal drop is 0.5 × 2 = 1 V. Subtract it from EMF to obtain 5 V at the terminals. The load calculation confirms this: 0.5 × 10 = 5 V.

questions.answer: The new current is 1 A and terminal voltage is 4 V. Compared with the preceding exercise, current rises from 0.5 A to 1 A while terminal voltage falls from 5 V to 4 V.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Keep EMF = 6 V and internal resistance = 2 Ω, but change the load from 10 Ω to 4 Ω. Calculate the new current and terminal voltage. Compare them with the preceding exercise.
questions.explanation: The new total is 4 + 2 = 6 Ω, so I = 6/6 = 1 A. Internal drop becomes 1 × 2 = 2 V, leaving V_terminal = 6 − 2 = 4 V. The load check gives 1 × 4 = 4 V. The smaller load resistance increases current, which increases the drop across the unchanged internal resistance.

questions.answer: The learner omitted the internal resistance. Including it gives I = 6/(4 + 2) = 1 A.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: For EMF = 6 V, internal resistance = 2 Ω, and load resistance = 4 Ω, a learner calculates I = 6/4 = 1.5 A. What model assumption has been omitted, and what is the correct current?
questions.explanation: The calculation assigns the full EMF to the external resistance and omits the internal series resistance. The denominator must be 4 + 2 = 6 Ω, giving I = 6/6 = 1 A. The 1.5 A answer would apply to a different model with zero internal resistance.

Interpret internal resistance and load resistance as series parts of the battery model.
Calculate load current using the sum of external and internal resistance.
Calculate internal voltage drop and loaded terminal voltage within the stated model.
Explain how load current affects terminal voltage without treating the simple model as a complete description of a real battery.

plan.goal: Read a sinusoidal cycle and distinguish peak, peak-to-peak and RMS voltage.
plan.focus: Locate the positive and negative extrema within a 0°–360° cycle and connect each amplitude measure to the diagram. Apply the source’s rounded conversion factors only to sine waves, with practice identifying the requested measure before calculating.
plan.title: Sinusoidal Waveforms and Amplitude Measures

lessons.title: Sinusoidal Waveforms and Amplitude Measures

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
Figure 5 on printed p. 19 shows one sinusoidal cycle from 0° to 360°. A cycle is one complete repetition of the waveform. The angle marks position within that repetition; it is not itself a voltage value or a time in seconds. The positive extremum occurs at 90°, and the negative extremum occurs at 270°. “Extremum” means an extreme value: the highest positive value or the lowest negative value.

Read the horizontal position and the vertical value separately. At 90°, the waveform reaches its positive peak; at 270°, it reaches its negative peak. These two positions are half a cycle apart. The negative peak is below the zero reference, but its distance from zero is a positive magnitude.

This lesson concerns the sinusoidal waveform and amplitude conversions verified on this page. It does not convert cycle angle into elapsed time or introduce other waveform shapes.
sections.heading: Read the cycle before reading its amplitude

sections.body:
Peak voltage, written V_p here, is the magnitude from the zero reference to an extreme of the sine wave. Peak-to-peak voltage, V_pp, is the full difference between the positive and negative extremes. Both quantities are expressed in volts (V), but they describe different spans on the waveform.

For the sine wave represented by the source, the positive and negative peak magnitudes are equal. Consequently, V_pp = 2V_p. Newly authored illustration: if the extremes are +4 V and −4 V, the peak magnitude is 4 V, while the peak-to-peak span is 4 − (−4) = 8 V. Subtracting a negative value adds its magnitude.

Before calculating, name the requested span: zero-to-extreme or extreme-to-extreme. Saying only “the amplitude is 8 V” can leave the measure unclear. Writing “8 V peak-to-peak” identifies it. Do not confuse a negative instantaneous voltage, such as −4 V, with a negative peak magnitude.
sections.heading: Peak and peak-to-peak measure different spans

sections.body:
RMS stands for root mean square. It is another way of specifying waveform amplitude, not the voltage at a particular angle and not the full positive-to-negative span. Write it as V_rms. The verified “Amplitude Conversion” material distinguishes RMS from peak and peak-to-peak voltage and supplies these rounded relations for a sine wave:

V_rms = 0.707V_p
V_p = 1.414V_rms
V_pp = 2.828V_rms
V_pp = 2V_p.

The multipliers are dimensionless: multiplying a voltage in volts by one of them still gives volts. For a nonzero sine wave, the magnitude ordering is V_rms < V_p < V_pp. This is a useful check, not a substitute for identifying the requested quantity.

These factors apply to sine waves. Do not use them as universal conversions for arbitrary waveforms. The extraction supplies conversion relations rather than a derivation of RMS, so this lesson practices their interpretation and use without claiming that the page establishes a general RMS calculation method.
sections.heading: RMS and the source’s sine-wave factors

sections.body:
The verified extraction supplies conversion factors but no complete numerical amplitude example to reproduce. The following worked examples are newly authored applications of those factors.

Example 1: a sine wave has V_p = 10 V. Find RMS and peak-to-peak voltage. Since the given value is peak, use V_rms = 0.707V_p: V_rms = 0.707 × 10 = 7.07 V. For peak-to-peak, V_pp = 2 × 10 = 20 V. The ordering 7.07 < 10 < 20 agrees with the expected magnitudes.

Example 2: a sine wave is specified as 5 V RMS. Find peak and peak-to-peak voltage. Use V_p = 1.414 × 5 = 7.07 V, then V_pp = 2.828 × 5 = 14.14 V. The alternative peak-to-peak check gives 2 × 7.07 = 14.14 V.

Keep the measure attached to each answer: 7.07 V peak and 14.14 V peak-to-peak are not interchangeable labels. These are written calculations, not instructions to generate or measure a waveform.
sections.heading: Worked conversions: identify the given measure first

sections.body:
When the supplied value is peak-to-peak, first recover peak voltage by dividing by two. This reverses V_pp = 2V_p. Newly authored example: for V_pp = 12 V, V_p = 12/2 = 6 V. Then V_rms = 0.707 × 6 = 4.242 V, or approximately 4.24 V.

You can also reverse the direct RMS relation: V_rms = V_pp/2.828. This gives 12/2.828 ≈ 4.243 V. The tiny difference between the two routes comes from using the source’s rounded factors. It is not evidence that peak-to-peak and RMS have changed meaning.

A reliable workflow is: label the given measure, label the requested measure, choose a relation connecting them, substitute with units, and check the magnitude ordering. Avoid presenting the rounded conversion factors as exact identities. Retain enough digits during the calculation, then round the final value to a sensible displayed precision.
sections.heading: Reverse conversions and rounding checks

questions.answer: The positive extremum is at 90° and the negative extremum is at 270°. The angles specify cycle position, not numerical voltage.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Within the source’s 0°–360° sinusoidal cycle, where are the positive and negative extrema? Do those angles specify voltage values?
questions.explanation: Figure 5 places the extrema at those cycle positions. An angle locates a point within the repetition; an amplitude specification is needed to assign its voltage value.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A sine wave reaches +3 V and −3 V. Find its peak magnitude and peak-to-peak voltage, showing the subtraction.
questions.explanation: Peak magnitude measures zero-to-extreme. Peak-to-peak measures the full span: 3 − (−3) = 6 V, also equal to 2V_p.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A sine wave has a peak voltage of 8 V. Calculate its RMS and peak-to-peak voltages using the source’s factors.
questions.explanation: V_rms = 0.707 × 8 = 5.656 V, rounded to 5.66 V. V_pp = 2 × 8 = 16 V. The resulting RMS magnitude is smaller than peak, while peak-to-peak is larger.

questions.answer: V_p ≈ 2.83 V peak; V_pp ≈ 5.66 V peak-to-peak.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A sine wave is specified as 2 V RMS. Find its peak and peak-to-peak voltages. Keep the amplitude labels in your answer.
questions.explanation: Use the RMS-to-peak factor: 1.414 × 2 = 2.828 V. For peak-to-peak, 2.828 × 2 = 5.656 V. Doubling the calculated peak provides the same peak-to-peak result.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A sine wave is 20 V peak-to-peak. Find peak voltage first, then RMS voltage.
questions.explanation: Reverse V_pp = 2V_p to obtain V_p = 20/2 = 10 V. Then V_rms = 0.707 × 10 = 7.07 V. Multiplying 20 directly by 0.707 would incorrectly treat the peak-to-peak value as peak.

questions.answer: The claim is incorrect. Peak and RMS are different measures; 6 V peak corresponds to approximately 4.24 V RMS.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A learner says, “A 6 V peak sine wave is also 6 V RMS because both are in volts.” Correct the claim and calculate the RMS value.
questions.explanation: Sharing a unit does not make the amplitude measures identical. The source’s sine-wave relation gives V_rms = 0.707 × 6 = 4.242 V, approximately 4.24 V.

questions.answer: No. That RMS result follows only if the waveform is sinusoidal; the shape has not been established.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A waveform is specified as 4 V peak, but its shape is not given. Can you conclude from this lesson that its RMS voltage is 2.828 V? Explain.
questions.explanation: The numerical product 0.707 × 4 is 2.828, but the cited conversion factor is specifically for a sine wave. Correct arithmetic cannot establish that an unsupported waveform assumption is valid.

objectives: Locate the positive and negative extrema within a sinusoidal cycle.
Distinguish peak voltage from peak-to-peak voltage.
Recognize RMS as a different amplitude measure rather than a point on the waveform.
Select and apply the verified sine-wave amplitude conversion factors.
Check conversion results for sensible magnitude and appropriate rounding.

plan.goal: Convert between period and frequency with correct seconds, hertz and metric prefixes.
plan.focus: Use T = 1/f and f = 1/T with explicit reciprocal entry and unit conversion. Check that increasing frequency decreases period, and treat the source’s 16.6 ms display for 60 Hz as rounded rather than exact.
plan.title: Period and Frequency Calculations

lessons.title: Period and Frequency Calculations

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Time and Frequency Conversion” material on printed p. 19 relates period and frequency as reciprocals. Period, written T, is the time for one cycle and is measured in seconds (s). Frequency, written f here, describes how many cycles occur per second and is measured in hertz (Hz). The source also uses capital F for frequency; this lesson consistently uses lowercase f.

The two relations are T = 1/f and f = 1/T. A reciprocal means one divided by a quantity—not that quantity divided by one. Thus, finding period from frequency means dividing 1 by the frequency. Finding frequency from period means dividing 1 by the period.

These quantities describe the same repetition from two viewpoints: the duration of one cycle and the number of cycles per second. This lesson is independent calculation practice; no prior lesson completion is assumed.
sections.heading: One repetition, two ways to describe it

sections.body:
Use frequency in hertz when you want T = 1/f to return period in seconds. Conversely, use period in seconds when you want f = 1/T to return frequency in hertz. Hertz corresponds to reciprocal seconds, so taking the reciprocal exchanges these units.

Newly authored worked example: find the period of a 50 Hz repetition. Write T = 1/f, then substitute T = 1/(50 Hz) = 0.02 s. This says that each cycle lasts two hundredths of a second. Check by multiplying the numerical values in the specified units: 50 × 0.02 = 1.

On a calculator, enter 1 ÷ 50. If using a reciprocal key, confirm that it performs 1 divided by the entered value. Entering 50 ÷ 1 leaves the frequency’s numerical value unchanged and does not calculate period. Keep the output unit beside the result: 0.02 s is a period, not a frequency.
sections.heading: Worked method: frequency to period

sections.body:
Newly authored worked example: a repetition has a period of 0.004 s. Find its frequency. Because the given quantity is period, choose f = 1/T. Substitute f = 1/(0.004 s) = 250 Hz.

The decimal 0.004 means four thousandths. Dividing 1 by a positive number smaller than 1 produces a number greater than 1; a result of 0.004 Hz would therefore indicate that the reciprocal was not taken. Check the calculation: 250 × 0.004 = 1.

The same relation gives a useful direction check. If period doubles while remaining positive, frequency halves: changing this example’s period from 0.004 s to 0.008 s gives 125 Hz. Equivalently, increasing frequency shortens period. These comparisons follow from the reciprocal formula; they are not additional source examples.
sections.heading: Worked method: period to frequency

sections.body:
The verified conversion examples on printed pp. 16–17 include 700 kHz = 700000 Hz = 0.7 MHz. They show that kilohertz values are multiplied by 1000 to obtain hertz and divided by 1000 to obtain megahertz. Preserve lowercase k and uppercase M in these prefixes.

Newly authored application: find the period at 2 kHz. First convert the frequency: 2 kHz = 2000 Hz. Then T = 1/2000 s = 0.0005 s. Taking 1/2 and labeling the result seconds would incorrectly treat 2 kHz as 2 Hz.

A prefix changes the numerical expression, not the frequency itself. As another application of the source’s verified conversion, 700 kHz and 0.7 MHz must give the same period because both are 700000 Hz. Their period is 1/700000 s ≈ 0.00000143 s. Converting to hertz before taking the reciprocal makes the output unit explicit and avoids prefix-related ambiguity.
sections.heading: Convert frequency units before taking the reciprocal

sections.body:
For 60 Hz, the reciprocal relation gives T = 1/60 s = 0.016666… s. Expressed in milliseconds, this is 16.666… ms, because one second contains 1000 milliseconds. The verified extraction flags the source’s displayed 16.6 ms as a limited-precision representation, not an exact equality. Written clearly, the result is approximately 16.6 ms at the source’s displayed precision; rounding to the nearest tenth of a millisecond instead gives 16.7 ms.

Keep the distinction between an exact relation and a rounded numerical result. T = 1/f is the relation; a shortened decimal generally needs an approximation sign. Retain enough digits during calculation and round the final answer rather than repeatedly rounding intermediate values.

For a final check, multiply frequency in hertz by period in seconds. The result should be 1, or close to 1 if the period has been rounded. Also ask whether the direction makes sense: higher frequency must mean less time per cycle.
sections.heading: Rounding and two useful checks

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A repetition has a frequency of 25 Hz. Find its period in seconds and verify the result by multiplication.
questions.explanation: Use T = 1/f = 1/25 = 0.04 s. The check is 25 × 0.04 = 1. The calculation finds time per cycle, so the answer is in seconds.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A period is 0.002 s. Find the frequency in hertz and then express it in kilohertz.
questions.explanation: First take the reciprocal: f = 1/0.002 = 500 Hz. Since 1000 Hz equals 1 kHz, divide the hertz value by 1000: 500 Hz = 0.5 kHz. Check with 500 × 0.002 = 1.

plan.goal: Relate capacitance and voltage to stored charge and electric-field energy.
plan.focus: Introduce farads, coulombs and joules, then apply Q = CV and the clear energy definition E = 0.5CV². Compare linear voltage dependence of charge with squared voltage dependence of energy. Use the verified charge example and avoid the unresolved notation in the source’s energy solution.
plan.title: Capacitor Charge and Stored Energy

lessons.title: Capacitor Charge and Stored Energy

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Capacitance” material in the left column of printed p. 20 relates a capacitor’s capacitance and voltage to its stored charge and electric-field energy. These are two different quantities: charge is measured in coulombs, while energy is measured in joules. A charge result cannot be relabeled as an energy result.

Define each symbol locally: Q is charge in coulombs (C); C in a formula is capacitance in farads (F); V is voltage in volts (V); and E in this lesson is stored energy in joules (J). In particular, the C in Q = CV means capacitance, not the coulomb unit. These notation distinctions are a brief reminder; the new focus is calculating and comparing charge and energy.

The accepted source formulas are Q = CV and E = 0.5CV². The extraction flags conflicting notation in the right-column energy solution. That solution is not used here. Energy calculations below are newly authored applications of the clear left-column definition, not reconstructed book examples.
sections.heading: Charge and energy are different stored quantities

sections.body:
The charge relation is Q = CV. Multiply capacitance in farads by voltage in volts to obtain charge in coulombs. For a fixed capacitance, this is a linear relationship: multiplying voltage by a factor multiplies charge by the same factor.

The verified charge example on printed p. 20 uses C = 5 µF and V = 12 V. Express the capacitance in farads before substituting: 5 µF = 5 × 10^-6 F = 0.000005 F. Then:

Q = CV
Q = (5 × 10^-6 F)(12 V)
Q = 60 × 10^-6 C = 60 µC.

The µ prefix in these expressions means one millionth. Thus 60 µC and 0.000060 C express the same charge. The intermediate multiplication is 5 × 12 = 60; the factor 10^-6 remains attached to the result.

Check by dividing the calculated charge by the voltage: (60 × 10^-6 C)/(12 V) = 5 × 10^-6 F, recovering the given capacitance. This reverse calculation follows from the same charge relation.
sections.heading: Verified source example: calculate charge

sections.body:
The clear energy definition on printed p. 20 is E = 0.5CV². Here 0.5 means one-half, and V² means voltage multiplied by itself. Only voltage is squared: the expression is not 0.5(CV)². Use C in farads and V in volts to obtain E in joules.

Newly authored worked calculation using the same numerical inputs as the verified charge example: let C = 5 µF and V = 12 V. This is an instructional application of the accepted energy definition, not a transcription of the disputed right-column solution.

First convert capacitance: C = 5 × 10^-6 F. Next square the voltage’s numerical value: 12² = 12 × 12 = 144. Substitute:

E = 0.5 × (5 × 10^-6) × 144 J
E = 360 × 10^-6 J = 360 µJ = 0.000360 J.

For these inputs, Q = 60 µC and E = 360 µJ. Keep both labels: the numbers describe different quantities in different units. All examples in this lesson are paper calculations, not construction or testing instructions.
sections.heading: Worked energy calculation: square voltage first

sections.body:
Compare the formulas while holding capacitance fixed. Charge contains V to the first power, so doubling voltage doubles Q. Energy contains V², so doubling voltage multiplies E by 2² = 4. Halving voltage halves charge but reduces energy to one-quarter. These comparisons are consequences of the source’s two accepted formulas.

Newly authored comparison: a 2 µF capacitor at 3 V has Q = (2 × 10^-6)(3) C = 6 µC and E = 0.5 × (2 × 10^-6) × 3² J = 9 µJ. At 6 V, the same capacitance gives Q = 12 µC and E = 36 µJ. The voltage doubles, charge doubles, and energy quadruples.

Now hold voltage fixed instead. Both formulas contain capacitance to the first power, so doubling capacitance doubles both charge and energy. State what is held fixed whenever making a comparison; otherwise, a change in capacitance could alter a conclusion based only on voltage.
sections.heading: Linear charge dependence and squared energy dependence

sections.body:
For each calculation, write the given capacitance and voltage, choose either the charge or energy relation, convert capacitance to farads, and retain the requested unit in the answer. For energy, show V² explicitly before multiplying. For charge, do not introduce a square that the formula does not contain.

Newly authored error check: for C = 4 µF and V = 5 V, Q = (4 × 10^-6)(5) C = 20 µC. Energy instead is E = 0.5 × (4 × 10^-6) × 25 J = 50 µJ. A proposed energy result of 10 µJ would come from using 5 rather than 5² and would omit the required square.

Use scaling as a second check: at fixed capacitance, a voltage increase by a factor of three must increase charge by three and energy by nine. Such checks can expose arithmetic or formula-selection errors, but they do not verify the original input values or resolve the source’s conflicting energy notation.
sections.heading: Check the formula, conversion and requested quantity

questions.answer: Q is charge in coulombs; C is capacitance in farads; V is voltage in volts; E is stored energy in joules. Voltage V is squared in the energy formula.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: In Q = CV and E = 0.5CV², identify each quantity and its unit. Which quantity is squared?
questions.explanation: The accepted p. 20 definitions distinguish charge from energy. C inside these equations is the capacitance symbol; it does not mean the coulomb unit. The exponent in the energy formula applies only to voltage.

questions.prompt: Practice using the verified source values: Calculate the charge for 5 µF at 12 V. Show the capacitance in farads and the answer in both coulombs and microcoulombs.
questions.explanation: Convert 5 µF to 5 × 10^-6 F, then use Q = CV: (5 × 10^-6)(12) = 60 × 10^-6 C. This reproduces the verified charge example.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A capacitor has C = 10 µF and V = 4 V. Calculate its charge and stored energy, showing the voltage square.

questions.answer: Q = 80 µC and E = 320 µJ. Charge doubles; energy quadruples.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Keep capacitance at 10 µF but increase voltage from 4 V to 8 V. Find the new charge and energy, and compare them with the preceding exercise.
questions.explanation: Q = (10 × 10^-6)(8) C = 80 µC. E = 0.5 × (10 × 10^-6) × 64 J = 320 µJ. At fixed capacitance, the doubled voltage doubles charge and quadruples energy.

questions.answer: Charge becomes one-half of its original value; energy becomes one-quarter.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A capacitor's voltage is halved while its capacitance remains fixed. What fraction of its original charge and energy remains?
questions.explanation: Replacing V with V/2 in Q = CV multiplies Q by 1/2. In E = 0.5CV², replacing V with V/2 multiplies E by (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.answer: The voltage square was omitted. The correct energy is 36 µJ.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: For 8 µF at 3 V, a learner calculates E = 0.5 × (8 × 10^-6) × 3 = 12 µJ. Identify the error and calculate the correct energy.
questions.explanation: The energy formula requires voltage squared. Use 3² = 9: E = 0.5 × (8 × 10^-6) × 9 J = 36 × 10^-6 J. The learner used the voltage only once.

questions.answer: The larger-capacitance capacitor has three times the charge and three times the energy, assuming the voltage is unchanged.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: At the same voltage, one capacitor has three times the capacitance of another. How do their charge and energy compare? State the assumption that makes the comparison valid.
questions.explanation: Both Q = CV and E = 0.5CV² contain capacitance to the first power. With the same voltage for both capacitors, multiplying capacitance by three multiplies both results by three.

Calculate stored charge using Q = CV with capacitance expressed in farads.
Calculate stored electric-field energy using E = 0.5CV².
Explain why doubling voltage doubles charge but quadruples energy at fixed capacitance.
Check conversions, squared quantities and the distinction between charge and energy.

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
Equivalent capacitance is the single total capacitance assigned to a stated capacitor combination. Write it as C_T, with C_1, C_2 and so on representing the individual capacitances. Capacitance is expressed in farads (F); the examples here use microfarads (µF). All values must be expressed in the same unit before combining them.

The verified “Capacitors in Series” material on printed p. 20 and its continuation on printed p. 21 establish two contrasting rules: parallel capacitances add directly, while series capacitances combine through reciprocals. Identify the arrangement before choosing the arithmetic. The same component values can produce different totals depending on their connection.

This lesson uses positive capacitance values and the simple series or parallel combinations specified in each exercise. It is written calculation practice, not a construction procedure. No prior lesson completion is required.
sections.heading: Identify the arrangement and define the total

sections.body:
For parallel capacitors, the source gives C_T = C_1 + C_2 + … + C_n. Add the capacitance values directly, keeping their shared unit.

The verified parallel example on printed p. 21 combines two 10 µF capacitors:
C_T = 10 µF + 10 µF = 20 µF.

Newly authored worked example: three parallel capacitors have values of 2 µF, 3 µF and 5 µF. Their total is C_T = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 µF. Because all inputs use microfarads, the sum is also in microfarads; conversion to farads is unnecessary for this addition.

A magnitude check follows from the formula: with two or more positive capacitances, a parallel total must exceed the largest individual value. In the newly authored example, 10 µF exceeds 5 µF. A result below 5 µF would contradict the stated parallel arrangement. This check is an instructional consequence of the verified rule, not an additional book example.
sections.heading: Parallel capacitance: add directly

sections.body:
For series capacitors, the verified rule is C_T = 1/(1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + … + 1/C_n). A reciprocal means one divided by a value. Keep the calculation in two stages: first add the individual reciprocals, then take the reciprocal of that entire sum.

Newly authored worked example: 3 µF and 6 µF are in series. Using microfarads consistently:
1/C_T = 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 0.5 µF^-1.
Then C_T = 1/(0.5 µF^-1) = 2 µF.

The intermediate 0.5 is not the final capacitance. Its unit is reciprocal microfarads, µF^-1; the final reciprocal restores microfarads. On a calculator, evaluate the complete denominator before dividing 1 by it.

For two or more positive series capacitances, the reciprocal sum exceeds the reciprocal of the smallest capacitance. Taking its reciprocal therefore gives a total below the smallest individual value. Here, 2 µF is below 3 µF, as expected.
sections.heading: Series capacitance: preserve both reciprocal stages

sections.body:
For exactly two series capacitors, the source supplies the convenient expression C_T = C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2). It is the same reciprocal rule written differently, not a separate physical relationship.

The algebra explains the shortcut: 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 = (C_1 + C_2)/(C_1C_2). Taking the reciprocal gives C_1C_2/(C_1 + C_2).

Newly authored worked example: combine 4 µF and 12 µF in series. First calculate the numerator, 4 × 12 = 48, and the denominator, 4 + 12 = 16. Then C_T = 48/16 = 3 µF. The product has units µF²; dividing by the sum in µF leaves µF.

Check with the full reciprocal method: 1/C_T = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 1/3 µF^-1, giving C_T = 3 µF. The answer is below 4 µF, the smaller input. Use product-over-sum for two capacitors only; for a larger series group, the general reciprocal sum remains available.
sections.heading: Two series capacitors: product over sum

sections.body:
For n equal capacitors in series, the source gives C_T = C/n, where C is the capacitance of each capacitor and n is the number of capacitors. The reciprocal sum explains why: n copies of 1/C add to n/C, whose reciprocal is C/n.

The verified series example on printed p. 20 uses three 10 µF capacitors:
C_T = 10/3 µF = 3.333… µF ≈ 3.3 µF.
The approximation sign matters because 3.3 µF is a shortened decimal representation, not the exact quotient.

Contrast this with the verified parallel example of two 10 µF capacitors, which gives 20 µF. For a direct same-count comparison, a newly authored application gives three 10 µF capacitors in parallel as 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 µF, rather than approximately 3.3 µF in series.

Check equality before using C/n. If the capacitors differ, dividing one selected capacitance by the number of capacitors is not supported by this shortcut.
sections.heading: Equal series capacitors and the source examples

sections.body:
The resistor rules on printed p. 19 provide a useful contrast: series resistances add, while parallel resistances use a reciprocal sum. Capacitors use the opposite arrangement-to-operation pairing: parallel capacitances add, while series capacitances use a reciprocal sum.

Do not transfer a resistor rule merely because a capacitor network has the same arrangement name. First identify the component type, then the connection, then the formula.

Newly authored comparison: two equal 8 µF capacitors give 16 µF in parallel and 4 µF in series. Two equal 8 Ω resistors give 16 Ω in series and 4 Ω in parallel. The arithmetic patterns match, but the arrangements and units do not.

A final capacitor check is therefore: parallel total above the largest individual capacitance; series total below the smallest, assuming at least two positive values. Then inspect the units and any rounding. These comparisons reinforce formula selection without requiring a repeat of resistor-network calculations.
sections.heading: Contrast with resistors and check the result

questions.answer: C_T = 7.9 µF, greater than the largest individual value.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Capacitors of 1 µF, 2.2 µF and 4.7 µF are connected in parallel. Calculate the total and give a magnitude check.
questions.explanation: Parallel capacitances add: 1 + 2.2 + 4.7 = 7.9 µF. For these positive values, the total must exceed the largest individual capacitance, 4.7 µF.

questions.answer: The reciprocal sum is 2/3 µF^-1; C_T = 1.5 µF.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Calculate the total of 2 µF and 6 µF in series using the reciprocal method. Show the intermediate unit.
questions.explanation: 1/C_T = 1/2 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 1/6 = 2/3 µF^-1. Taking the reciprocal gives C_T = 3/2 = 1.5 µF. It is below the smaller input, 2 µF.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Find the equivalent capacitance of 5 µF and 20 µF in series using product-over-sum.
questions.explanation: C_T = (5 × 20)/(5 + 20) = 100/25 = 4 µF. The result is smaller than 5 µF, consistent with the series rule for positive capacitances.

questions.prompt: Practice using the verified source values: Three 10 µF capacitors are connected in series. Give the exact quotient and an approximate result to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The capacitors are equal, so C_T = C/n = 10/3 µF. Its decimal value is 3.333… µF, which rounds to 3.3 µF. This reproduces the verified series example.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Capacitors of 6 µF, 3 µF and 2 µF are connected in series. Calculate their total.
questions.explanation: 1/C_T = 1/6 + 1/3 + 1/2 = 1/6 + 2/6 + 3/6 = 1 µF^-1. Its reciprocal is 1 µF, below the smallest individual value of 2 µF.

questions.answer: The learner used the parallel rule. The correct series total is 6 µF.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A learner adds two 12 µF series capacitors and reports 24 µF. Identify the incorrect rule and calculate the correct total.
questions.explanation: Direct addition is the capacitor parallel rule, not the capacitor series rule. Two equal series capacitors give C_T = C/n = 12/2 = 6 µF.

questions.answer: The final reciprocal is missing. The intermediate unit is µF^-1; the correct total is 2 µF.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: For 4 µF and 4 µF in series, a learner reports the reciprocal sum, 0.5, as 0.5 µF. What step and unit distinction are missing?
questions.explanation: 1/4 + 1/4 = 0.5 µF^-1 represents 1/C_T. Taking its reciprocal gives C_T = 1/0.5 = 2 µF. The equal-series shortcut confirms 4/2 = 2 µF.

questions.answer: Capacitors add directly in parallel; resistors add directly in series. The component type determines which arrangement-to-operation rule applies.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Which arrangement uses direct addition for capacitors, and which uses direct addition for resistors? Why should you identify the component type before selecting a rule?
questions.explanation: The verified rules assign direct addition to parallel capacitances and series resistances. Their reciprocal rules apply to the opposite arrangements, so arrangement alone is not enough to choose the operation.

objectives: Calculate parallel capacitance by adding individual capacitances.
Calculate series capacitance by taking the reciprocal of a sum of reciprocals.
Use product-over-sum for two series capacitors and C/n for equal series capacitors.
Distinguish capacitor-combination rules from resistor-combination rules.
Check equivalent capacitance against the individual capacitor values.

plan.goal: Calculate an RC time constant and explain its role in exponential capacitor charging and discharging.
plan.focus: Use TC = RC with ohms and farads, reproduce the 0.05 s example and interpret the verified 63.2 V charging value after one time constant with 100 V applied. plan.title: RC Time Constants and Exponential Response

lessons.title: RC Time Constants and Exponential Response

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Time Constants” material on printed p. 21 describes exponential capacitor charging and discharging and defines one RC time constant as resistance multiplied by capacitance. An RC response combines resistance, written R, and capacitance, written C. Here R is measured in ohms (Ω), and C is measured in farads (F).

Write the time constant as TC, following the extracted formula: TC = RC. TC is a time, measured in seconds (s). It provides a characteristic timescale for the response, not a statement that charging or discharging is complete at that instant.

The capacitor charge relation on printed p. 20 is Q = CV, where Q is charge in coulombs and V is capacitor voltage in volts. For fixed capacitance, charge and capacitor voltage change together. This connection helps explain why a discussion of capacitor charging can describe voltage as it changes over time. The new focus here is the timing of that change, not a repeat of charge or energy calculations.
sections.heading: What an RC time constant describes

sections.body:
The verified worked values on printed p. 21 use R = 10 kΩ and C = 5 µF. Convert both to the units required by TC = RC:

R = 10 kΩ = 10000 Ω = 10^4 Ω.
C = 5 µF = 0.000005 F = 5 × 10^-6 F.

Now substitute:
TC = RC
TC = 10000 × 0.000005 s
TC = 0.05 s.

Equivalently, multiply the powers of ten: 10^4 × 5 × 10^-6 = 5 × 10^-2 = 0.05. The result is five hundredths of a second, or 50 milliseconds (ms). One millisecond is one thousandth of a second.

The unit combination Ω·F corresponds to seconds in this relation. Do not multiply the displayed numbers 10 and 5 and label the result 50 seconds: that would ignore the kilo and micro scale factors. Writing the converted quantities before multiplication makes the scale visible. The calculation reproduces the accepted source result; it does not use the disputed timing labels in Figure 6.
sections.heading: Verified worked example: 10 kΩ and 5 µF

sections.body:
The accepted charging example on printed p. 21 gives a capacitor voltage of 63.2 V after one charging time constant with 100 V applied. The ratio is 63.2/100 = 0.632, so the displayed capacitor voltage is 63.2% of the applied voltage at that point in the example.

This illustrates why one time constant is not a completion time. At that instant, the difference between the applied voltage and capacitor voltage is still 100 − 63.2 = 36.8 V. Keep these quantities separate: 100 V is the applied voltage, 63.2 V is the capacitor voltage, and 36.8 V is their remaining difference.

For the verified resistance and capacitance calculation, one time constant is 0.05 s. The accepted examples therefore connect a characteristic time of 0.05 s with the stated one-time-constant charging value. The 63.2 V value is a displayed numerical result, not an exact universal voltage independent of the applied voltage or charging conditions.

These are paper calculations only. The extraction does not supply a laboratory procedure for constructing or testing the 100 V example.
sections.heading: Interpret the one-time-constant charging value

sections.body:
An exponential response does not change by the same number of volts during every equal time interval. In charging, the capacitor voltage approaches its final level with progressively smaller changes. In discharging, it falls toward its final level with progressively smaller changes. Thus a straight-line assumption—such as adding the first interval’s voltage increase repeatedly—does not represent the response described by the source.

A larger TC means a longer characteristic timescale; a smaller TC means a shorter one. This comparison concerns timing, not a change in the definition of voltage or charge. For fixed capacitance, Q = CV also means that the changing charge follows the changing capacitor voltage.

The extraction flags Figure 6’s first discharge percentage and final time-marker label as questionable. It also flags the unqualified claim of complete charging after five time constants. Those items are not adopted here. We will not use that graph to assign numerical discharge percentages, nor claim exact completion at five time constants. The accepted evidence supports exponential behavior and the stated charging result, but this lesson does not reconstruct a full response table or add an unextracted response equation.
sections.heading: Exponential response and the limits of the evidence

sections.body:
The product TC = RC makes timing comparisons straightforward. Holding capacitance fixed, doubling resistance doubles the time constant. Holding resistance fixed, doubling capacitance also doubles it. If both are doubled, the product becomes four times as large. State what remains fixed when making any such comparison.

Newly authored worked example: let R = 2000 Ω and C = 10 × 10^-6 F. Then TC = 2000 × 10 × 10^-6 s = 0.02 s. Increasing resistance to 4000 Ω while keeping capacitance unchanged gives TC = 0.04 s. The characteristic response time doubles.

For another newly authored comparison, doubling resistance while halving capacitance leaves the product unchanged: (2R)(C/2) = RC. This is an algebraic timing comparison, not a claim that every feature of the two circuits is identical.

A useful workflow is to convert the units, multiply R by C, label the result in seconds, and then compare it with the original values. Any response interpretation should remain separate from the arithmetic: calculating TC alone does not establish a complete voltage-versus-time curve.
sections.heading: Newly authored practice method: compare the RC product

questions.prompt: Practice using the verified source values: Calculate TC for 10 kΩ and 5 µF. Show both conversions and give the result in seconds and milliseconds.
questions.explanation: Convert resistance to 10000 Ω and capacitance to 5 × 10^-6 F. Their product is 0.05 s. Multiplying seconds by 1000 expresses the same time as 50 ms.

questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: Find the time constant for R = 20 kΩ and C = 2 µF.
questions.explanation: Use ohms and farads: R = 20000 Ω and C = 2 × 10^-6 F. TC = 20000 × 2 × 10^-6 = 0.04 s. This is a characteristic time, not a completion time.

questions.answer: The capacitor voltage is 63.2% of the applied voltage; the remaining difference is 36.8 V.
questions.prompt: Practice interpreting the verified charging example: With 100 V applied, the capacitor voltage is 63.2 V after one time constant. What percentage of the applied voltage is this, and what voltage difference remains?
questions.explanation: The percentage is (63.2/100) × 100% = 63.2%. Subtract capacitor voltage from applied voltage: 100 − 63.2 = 36.8 V. A nonzero difference remains, so one time constant does not indicate completion.

questions.answer: The new time constant is 0.09 s.
questions.prompt: Newly authored practice: A response has TC = 0.03 s. Resistance is tripled while capacitance remains unchanged. What is the new time constant?
