sections.body:
The “Capacitive Reactance” material on printed p. 21 describes a capacitor’s opposition to alternating current as capacitive reactance. Write this quantity as X_C, where the subscript C identifies the capacitive case. Reactance is measured in ohms (Ω).

The source gives X_C = 1/(2πfC). Here f is frequency in hertz (Hz), C is capacitance in farads (F), and π is the dimensionless mathematical constant pi, approximately 3.14159. C inside this equation represents capacitance, not the coulomb unit.

Unlike a fixed numerical resistance value, the reactance calculated by this expression depends on frequency as well as capacitance. Consequently, a capacitance value alone is insufficient to determine X_C: the frequency must also be specified.

This lesson applies the formula to positive frequency and capacitance values and interprets the source’s sinusoidal phase diagrams. It does not extend the calculation into an arbitrary network or a general waveform analysis.
sections.heading: What capacitive reactance measures

sections.body:
Read the formula as one divided by the entire product 2πfC. Calculate that denominator first, then take its reciprocal. It is not equivalent to dividing by 2π and subsequently multiplying by f and C.

The verified extraction supplies the formula but no numerical reactance example to reproduce. The following is newly authored practice: find X_C for f = 1000 Hz and C = 1 µF.

First convert capacitance: 1 µF = 1 × 10^-6 F. Substitute:
X_C = 1/[2π × 1000 × (1 × 10^-6)] Ω.
The frequency–capacitance product is 1000 × 10^-6 = 0.001. Thus the denominator is 2π × 0.001 ≈ 0.00628319, and X_C ≈ 159.15 Ω, or approximately 159 Ω.

On a calculator, use parentheses around the whole denominator: 1 ÷ (2 × π × 1000 × 0.000001). Retain intermediate digits and round the final result. The units Hz and F combine so that the reciprocal expression returns ohms; the final value is a reactance, not a capacitance or frequency.
sections.heading: Worked calculation: evaluate the complete denominator

sections.body:
Frequency appears in the denominator of X_C = 1/(2πfC). Holding capacitance fixed, increasing frequency increases the denominator and decreases reactance. Doubling frequency therefore halves X_C; halving frequency doubles it.

Newly authored comparison using C = 1 µF: at 1000 Hz, the preceding calculation gives X_C ≈ 159.15 Ω. At 2000 Hz, X_C = 1/[2π × 2000 × 10^-6] Ω ≈ 79.58 Ω. The doubled frequency produces half the reactance.

Capacitance also appears in the denominator. Holding frequency fixed, doubling capacitance halves reactance. For example, at 1000 Hz, increasing capacitance from 1 µF to 2 µF gives approximately 79.58 Ω instead of 159.15 Ω.

These are consequences of the verified formula, not additional source examples. Always state what remains fixed. If both frequency and capacitance double, the denominator becomes four times larger and reactance becomes one-quarter as large. A direction check can reveal an error: with one input fixed, a larger value of the other should not produce a larger X_C.
sections.heading: Frequency and capacitance have inverse effects

sections.body:
The waveform views in Figure 7 on printed p. 21 show capacitor current leading capacitor voltage by 90°. “Leading” describes relative position within the sinusoidal cycle: corresponding points on the current waveform occur one-quarter of a cycle before those on the voltage waveform. A full cycle is 360°, so 90° is one-quarter of that cycle.

This is a comparison between two changing quantities, not a statement that current has a larger amplitude than voltage. Current and voltage have different units, and a phase difference does not specify their numerical amplitudes. Nor does “90°” mean 90 seconds: it expresses cycle position.

A useful verbal reading is: current is ahead of voltage by a quarter-cycle; equivalently, voltage lags current by a quarter-cycle. Reversing which quantity leads would reverse the source’s stated relationship.

Keep two questions separate. X_C answers how much capacitive opposition the formula assigns at a stated frequency and capacitance. The 90° relationship answers how current and voltage are positioned relative to each other in the source’s sinusoidal representation.
sections.heading: Read current leading voltage by 90°

sections.body:
Figure 7 also represents the phase relationship with phasors: the current arrow points right, and the voltage arrow points downward. In this introductory view, a phasor is an arrow used to display the relative phase of a sinusoidal quantity. The two arrows are perpendicular, representing a 90° separation.

For the source’s particular sketch, read the arrow positions together with its stated relationship: current leads voltage by 90°. The downward voltage arrow does not mean that capacitor voltage is permanently negative. Similarly, the right-pointing current arrow is not a drawing of current physically flowing toward the right in a circuit. These are phase-reference directions.

The waveform and phasor views present the same relationship in different forms: one shows variation across a cycle, while the other condenses relative phase into arrow directions. This lesson does not infer arrow-length scales that are absent from the extraction or introduce complex-number calculations.

A calculated result such as X_C ≈ 159 Ω is a positive reactance magnitude in this formula. It does not replace the separate statement that current leads voltage. Reporting both magnitude and phase relationship preserves the two distinct pieces of information.
sections.heading: Connect the waveform and phasor views

sections.body:
The “Inductance” material on printed p. 22 describes inductance as opposition to changes in current. Inductance is measured in henrys, abbreviated H. Use L as the symbol for an inductance value in this lesson. A millihenry, written mH, is one thousandth of a henry: 4 mH = 0.004 H.

The word “changes” matters. Saying that inductance opposes changing current is not the same as saying that it simply prevents current from flowing. The source identifies a response to current changing, rather than defining inductance as an ordinary resistance value. Keep the quantity and unit distinct: an inductance value is expressed in henrys, not ohms.

This lesson focuses on inductance and component combinations. The page also discusses frequency-dependent inductive reactance, but calculating that separate quantity is outside this selected unit. An inductance value such as 4 mH should not be relabeled as a reactance value.

All examples here are written calculations. No construction, measurement procedure, or learner completion requirement is implied.
sections.heading: Inductance concerns changes in current

sections.body:
The verified simple series example on printed p. 22 combines three 4 mH inductors and gives 12 mH. Its arithmetic is direct addition:

L_total = 4 mH + 4 mH + 4 mH = 12 mH.

Here L_total names the equivalent inductance of the stated combination. All terms use the same unit, so the sum remains in millihenrys. A unit check gives the same result in henrys: 0.004 + 0.004 + 0.004 = 0.012 H = 12 mH.

For written practice, direct addition will be used only in a stated simple model that neglects mutual-inductance effects. That assumption is important: the same source discussion distinguishes reinforcing and opposing magnetic fields and introduces a mutual-inductance adjustment. Therefore, the numerical example must not be turned into an unconditional claim that every set of series inductors has a total equal to the sum of its individual values.

Newly authored application under the stated simple model: two 3 mH inductors in series give 3 + 3 = 6 mH. This is instructional arithmetic, not another extracted book example.
sections.heading: The source’s simple series example

sections.body:
The verified simple parallel example on printed p. 22 gives approximately 1.3 mH for three 4 mH inductors. The upper-right wording is partly cropped, so this lesson uses the accepted numerical result without reconstructing the missing text.

For the equal-inductor practice model used here, neglect mutual-inductance effects and divide the individual inductance by the number of equal parallel inductors:

L_total = L/n,

where L is each individual inductance and n is the number of equal inductors. With L = 4 mH and n = 3, L_total = 4/3 mH = 1.333… mH ≈ 1.3 mH, matching the accepted source result. The approximation sign distinguishes the displayed decimal from the exact quotient.

Newly authored application of this explicitly limited model: three equal 6 mH inductors in parallel give 6/3 = 2 mH. Do not use this practice shortcut for unequal inductors or for an unspecified magnetically coupled arrangement.

The extraction does not fully establish the coupling assumptions behind the source’s parallel discussion. We therefore do not teach a general coupled-inductor parallel formula from it.
sections.heading: The simple parallel example and its limits

sections.body:
The series-inductor discussion on printed p. 22 distinguishes magnetic fields that reinforce from fields that oppose and introduces mutual inductance as an adjustment to the simple combination calculation. Reinforcing means that the magnetic-field contributions support one another; opposing means that they act against one another. These are different relationships, so they cannot be ignored when the source says a mutual-inductance adjustment is involved.

The useful conceptual distinction is between an isolated arithmetic model and a combination whose magnetic interaction matters. Knowing only the individual inductance values and the word “series” or “parallel” does not always establish the equivalent inductance when mutual effects are present.

The verified extraction does not supply enough detail to calculate a general coupled arrangement or reconstruct every adjustment. This lesson therefore does not invent a mutual-inductance equation, coupling value, or connection diagram.

Before calculating, ask: Are the inductors in series or parallel? Are their values equal if using the equal-parallel shortcut? Does the problem explicitly permit neglecting mutual effects? If that last assumption is absent and coupling matters, state the limitation rather than reporting an unsupported total.

sections.body:
The “Inductive Reactance” material on printed p. 22 gives a frequency-dependent expression for an inductor’s opposition to alternating current. Write inductive reactance as X_L, where the subscript L identifies the inductive case. Reactance is measured in ohms (Ω), whereas inductance itself is measured in henrys (H).

The source gives X_L = 2πfL. Here f is frequency in hertz (Hz), L is inductance in henrys, and π is the dimensionless mathematical constant pi, approximately 3.14159. Use frequency in hertz and inductance in henrys to obtain reactance in ohms.

Inductance and inductive reactance are not interchangeable quantities. An inductance of 10 mH identifies L; it does not identify X_L until a frequency is supplied. The same inductance gives different reactance values at different frequencies.

The examples below assume positive frequency and inductance values and apply the source’s component formula. They are written calculations, not construction or measurement instructions. Their results should not be treated as the impedance of an unspecified complete circuit.
sections.heading: Inductance and reactance have different units

sections.body:
The verified extraction supplies the inductive-reactance formula but no complete numerical example to reproduce. This worked example is newly authored: find X_L for f = 1000 Hz and L = 10 mH.

First convert inductance to henrys. The milli prefix means one thousandth, so 10 mH = 10 × 10^-3 H = 0.010 H. Substitute:

X_L = 2πfL
X_L = 2π × 1000 × 0.010 Ω
X_L = 20π Ω ≈ 62.83 Ω.

The intermediate product fL is 1000 × 0.010 = 10. Multiplying by 2π then gives approximately 62.83. On a calculator, enter 2 × π × 1000 × 0.010; do not take the reciprocal. Keep enough intermediate digits and round the final answer.

If the frequency is supplied as 1 kHz, convert it to 1000 Hz before this substitution. If 10 mH is incorrectly entered as 10 H, the inductance is made 1000 times too large and the calculated reactance is also 1000 times too large. Writing both converted inputs explicitly helps expose these errors.
sections.heading: Worked calculation with explicit unit conversions

sections.body:
In X_L = 2πfL, both frequency and inductance are multiplying factors. Holding inductance fixed, doubling frequency doubles reactance. Holding frequency fixed, doubling inductance also doubles reactance. If both double, reactance becomes four times as large. These are consequences of the verified formula, not additional extracted source examples.

Newly authored comparison: retain L = 0.010 H but increase frequency from 1000 Hz to 2000 Hz. The new result is X_L = 2π × 2000 × 0.010 Ω = 40π Ω ≈ 125.66 Ω. This is twice the preceding 62.83 Ω result, allowing for displayed rounding.

The capacitive formula on printed p. 21 is X_C = 1/(2πfC), with C in farads. Frequency appears in its denominator, so doubling frequency at fixed capacitance halves capacitive reactance. Thus increasing frequency increases X_L but decreases X_C when the respective component values are fixed.

This comparison concerns individual reactance magnitudes. It does not, by itself, determine the behavior of an arbitrary circuit containing both components.
sections.heading: Direct inductive scaling versus inverse capacitive scaling

sections.body:
The text and Figure 9 on printed p. 22 show voltage leading current in the inductive case. “Leading” describes relative position in the waveform cycle: corresponding features of the voltage waveform occur ahead of those of the current waveform. Equivalently, current lags voltage.

This statement does not mean that voltage has a larger amplitude than current. Voltage and current have different units, and a phase relationship is not an amplitude comparison. It also does not mean that an inductor’s voltage must always be positive.

The supplied S14 evidence verifies which quantity leads, but it does not specify a numerical inductive phase angle. Therefore, this lesson does not assign a degree value or a fraction of a cycle to that lead. A numerical angle would require further verification of the printed source.

For comparison, the capacitive evidence on printed p. 21 explicitly states that current leads voltage by 90°. Preserve the distinction in evidence: the inductive case supports “voltage leads current”; the capacitive case supports “current leads voltage by 90°.” Do not transfer the capacitive numerical angle into the inductive statement.
sections.heading: Voltage leads current: what the evidence establishes

sections.body:
Reactance magnitude and phase answer different questions. The formula X_L = 2πfL gives a numerical opposition in ohms at a stated frequency and inductance. The voltage-leading statement identifies the relative waveform order. Calculating one does not replace reporting the other.

Newly authored reporting example: for a 10 mH inductor at 1000 Hz, write, “The inductive reactance is approximately 62.83 Ω; the source’s inductive representation shows voltage leading current.” This gives both the calculated magnitude and the verified qualitative phase relationship without inventing an angle.

A reliable calculation workflow is to identify the component, write its formula, convert the inputs to hertz and henrys, substitute, and label the answer in ohms. Then report phase separately using only the relationship established by the evidence.

For a final direction check, ask what changed. At fixed inductance, a higher frequency must produce a higher X_L. At fixed frequency, a lower inductance must produce a lower X_L. If your result goes the opposite way, check for an accidental reciprocal or a missed prefix conversion.

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Impedance” example on printed p. 23 combines resistance, inductive reactance and capacitive reactance in a series-RLC circuit. Here “RLC” identifies the resistive, inductive and capacitive parts. Define R as resistance, X_L as inductive reactance, X_C as capacitive reactance, and Z as impedance magnitude. All four values in this calculation are expressed in ohms (Ω).

The verified formula is:
Z = √((X_C − X_L)² + R²).

The square root covers the entire sum, including both squared terms. Z here is a magnitude: it describes the size of the combined opposition, not whether the circuit is predominantly capacitive or inductive.

Use this expression for the stated series-RLC arrangement. This lesson does not provide a general parallel-network expression or a method for arbitrary mixed networks. Its examples assume that resistance and both reactances are already supplied for the same operating frequency.
sections.heading: Define the series-circuit quantities

sections.body:
The source’s phase descriptions explain why the reactive contributions must be distinguished rather than simply added as positive numbers. Printed p. 21 shows capacitor current leading voltage by 90°. Printed p. 22 shows inductor voltage leading current. These are different current–voltage relationships. The series example on p. 23 combines their opposing reactive contributions through a difference.

For this lesson, define a calculation quantity D = X_C − X_L, in ohms. This is an instructional label for the difference used in the source formula, not a new source symbol.

If X_C exceeds X_L, D is positive under this chosen subtraction order and the circuit is predominantly capacitive. If X_L exceeds X_C, D is negative and the circuit is predominantly inductive. If the values are equal, D is zero.

The sign depends on which subtraction order you choose. Therefore, report predominance with words and the original reactance comparison, rather than relying on an unexplained sign. The supplied inductive evidence does not specify a numerical phase angle, and this lesson does not infer a circuit phase angle.
sections.heading: Interpret the reactive difference before squaring

sections.body:
After calculating D = X_C − X_L, the magnitude calculation becomes Z = √(D² + R²). Squaring makes D² nonnegative, whether D was positive or negative. Thus the same resistance and the same absolute reactive difference produce the same impedance magnitude even when the predominant reactive type differs.

The p. 23 phasor sketch accompanies the source’s predominantly capacitive example. Use the sketch as a representation of the combination, not as a picture of physical current direction. The square-and-square-root expression combines the resistive contribution with the net reactive contribution; it is not ordinary addition of their magnitudes.

For example, a reactive difference of 4 Ω and resistance of 3 Ω produce √(4² + 3²) = 5 Ω, not 4 + 3 = 7 Ω. The squared terms have units Ω², and taking the square root restores Ω.

A useful formula-derived check is Z ≥ R and Z ≥ |D| for nonnegative resistance. A result smaller than either contribution indicates an arithmetic or formula-entry error.
sections.heading: Magnitude combines squared contributions

sections.body:
The verified worked example on printed p. 23 uses R = 3 Ω, X_L = 16 Ω and X_C = 20 Ω. First compare the reactances: 20 Ω exceeds 16 Ω, so the circuit is predominantly capacitive, as identified by the source’s phasor sketch.

Next calculate the difference:
D = X_C − X_L = 20 − 16 = 4 Ω.

Substitute into the magnitude formula:
Z = √((20 − 16)² + 3²) Ω
Z = √(4² + 3²) Ω
Z = √(16 + 9) Ω
Z = √25 Ω = 5 Ω.

The result is 5 Ω impedance magnitude, with capacitive predominance. These are two separate pieces of information. The calculation passes the magnitude checks: 5 Ω is greater than both the 3 Ω resistance and the 4 Ω reactive difference.

Do not add 3 + 16 + 20, and do not stop after finding the difference. The first would ignore the source’s reactive opposition and magnitude formula; the second would omit the resistance contribution.
sections.heading: Verified example: 3 Ω, 16 Ω and 20 Ω

sections.body:
Newly authored worked comparison: retain R = 3 Ω but exchange the reactances, so X_L = 20 Ω and X_C = 16 Ω. Now D = 16 − 20 = −4 Ω. Since inductive reactance is larger, the circuit is predominantly inductive.

Calculate magnitude separately:
Z = √((−4)² + 3²) Ω
Z = √(16 + 9) Ω = 5 Ω.

The magnitude matches the source example, but the predominance does not. Squaring removes the difference’s sign; it does not erase the physical distinction expressed by the reactance comparison. In particular, (−4)² = 16, not −16.

For another newly authored case, let R = 8 Ω and both reactances equal 12 Ω. Their difference is zero, so the formula gives Z = √(0² + 8²) = 8 Ω. Neither reactance predominates in this calculation.

Use the workflow: identify the series arrangement, compare reactances, calculate their difference, square both contributions, add, take the square root, and report magnitude plus predominance. These are paper calculations, not circuit-building instructions.

lessons.title: Resonance and Resonant Frequency

source.title: Associate CET Study Guide Chapter 3 : Math For Electronics

sections.body:
The “Resonance” material on printed p. 23 identifies resonance through equality of inductive and capacitive reactance: X_L = X_C. Here X_L is inductive reactance and X_C is capacitive reactance, both measured in ohms (Ω). The source’s numerical example is explicitly a series circuit; this lesson retains that context.

The equality concerns the two reactance magnitudes at the same frequency. It does not say that inductance and capacitance are equal: those are different quantities, measured in henrys and farads. Nor does it say that voltage and current are equal numerical quantities.

The component formulas explain why the equality can occur. With component values fixed, X_L = 2πfL increases as frequency increases, while X_C = 1/(2πfC) decreases. Resonant frequency, written f_r, is the frequency at which these magnitudes match.

The extraction flags a source current claim that does not clearly distinguish series from parallel conditions. This lesson therefore teaches the verified equality and frequency calculation, not a general maximum-current claim or a parallel-resonance rule.
sections.heading: Resonance: equal reactances at one frequency

sections.body:
Define L as inductance in henrys (H), C as capacitance in farads (F), and f_r as resonant frequency in hertz (Hz). The constant π is dimensionless and approximately 3.14159. Assume positive L and C values.

Substitute the component formulas into the resonance condition:
2πf_rL = 1/(2πf_rC).

Multiply both sides by 2πf_rC to remove the denominator:
(2πf_r)²LC = 1.

Divide by 4π²LC:
f_r² = 1/(4π²LC).

Taking the positive square root gives the verified formula:
f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)).

The positive root is chosen because the frequency here is positive. The radical covers the product LC only; 2π multiplies that square root outside it. Evaluate LC first, then its square root, then the full denominator, and finally its reciprocal.

This algebra connects the source’s accepted equations. It does not introduce a new circuit model. C inside the formula is capacitance, not the coulomb unit, and f_r is a frequency rather than a farad abbreviation.
sections.heading: From reactance equality to the frequency formula

sections.body:
The source’s series example on printed p. 23, with its solution continuing on p. 24, uses L = 200 µH and C = 200 pF and reports approximately 795 kHz. Convert the values before substituting:

L = 200 × 10^-6 H = 2 × 10^-4 H.
C = 200 × 10^-12 F = 2 × 10^-10 F.

Multiply:
LC = (2 × 10^-4)(2 × 10^-10) H·F = 4 × 10^-14 H·F.

Take the square root of the entire product:
√(LC) = 2 × 10^-7 s.

Now evaluate the denominator and reciprocal:
2π√(LC) ≈ 1.256637 × 10^-6 s.
f_r ≈ 1/(1.256637 × 10^-6 s) ≈ 795775 Hz.

Thus the independently recalculated result is approximately 795.8 kHz, or 796 kHz to the nearest kilohertz. The source reports approximately 795 kHz; retain that as its reported result rather than claiming it is nearest-kilohertz rounding of this calculation.

The unit check matters: H·F has the dimensions of seconds squared, so √(LC) has dimensions of seconds. Taking the reciprocal of the denominator therefore returns hertz.
sections.heading: Verified example with an independent calculation

sections.body:
A useful independent check is to substitute the calculated resonant frequency into both reactance formulas. Using the unrounded result from the source-value calculation, f_r ≈ 795774.7 Hz:

X_L = 2πf_rL
≈ 2π × 795774.7 × (2 × 10^-4) Ω
≈ 1000 Ω.

X_C = 1/(2πf_rC)
≈ 1/[2π × 795774.7 × (2 × 10^-10)] Ω
≈ 1000 Ω.

The matching values confirm the defining equality. Small differences can appear if a rounded frequency is used; keep intermediate digits when checking.

This check is a newly authored application of the verified component formulas, not an additional transcribed source solution. It checks the resonance calculation without claiming a circuit current, voltage amplitude or phase angle.

If the two reactances differ substantially, inspect the prefix conversions and calculator parentheses. In particular, 200 µH is not 200 H, and 200 pF is not 200 F. Both formulas must use the same frequency in hertz.
sections.heading: Check resonance by calculating both reactances

sections.body:
The formula f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) provides a direction check. Increasing either L or C while holding the other fixed increases the denominator and lowers resonant frequency. The square root makes the relationship different from simple inverse proportionality.

Newly authored comparison: if inductance becomes four times as large while capacitance stays fixed, LC becomes four times as large, √(LC) doubles, and f_r halves. If both inductance and capacitance double, their product becomes four times as large, so resonant frequency again halves.

Newly authored worked example: let L = 1 mH = 10^-3 H and C = 1 nF = 10^-9 F. Then LC = 10^-12 H·F and √(LC) = 10^-6 s. Therefore f_r = 1/(2π × 10^-6 s) ≈ 159155 Hz ≈ 159.2 kHz.

For any calculation, record the arrangement and assumptions, convert to henrys and farads, multiply, take the square root, form the denominator and take its reciprocal. Check the units and the expected direction of change. These are paper calculations, not construction or testing instructions.

overview.reveal: A negative exponent gives a reciprocal: 10⁻³ = 1/10³ = 0.001.

overview.outcome: Use powers of ten and prefixes to keep the same electrical quantity while changing its written scale.

sections.body:
Think of 1,000 milliamperes and 1 ampere as two labels for the same current. The prefix tells you the scale used by the number beside it. Kilo means 10³, milli means 10⁻³, micro means 10⁻⁶, and pico means 10⁻¹².

Before entering a value into a formula, read the complete label. A value of 5 mA is not the same as 5 A. Convert the number and its unit together: 5 mA = 5 × 10⁻³ A = 0.005 A. The current has not become smaller; you have expressed it in a larger unit.
sections.heading: A prefix changes the label, not the quantity

sections.body:
Scientific notation separates a manageable leading number from a scale factor. In 1.25 × 10⁵, the 10⁵ multiplies 1.25 by 100,000, giving 125,000. A negative exponent means a reciprocal: 10⁻³ = 1/1,000. So 7 × 10⁻³ is 0.007.

Keep the leading number between 1 and 10 when writing normalized scientific notation. If you move the decimal in the leading number, compensate with the exponent so the original value stays unchanged. This is a way to organize place value, not permission to drop zeros arbitrarily.
sections.heading: Why scientific notation helps

sections.body:
The source example starts with 1,000 pF. Convert to farads first: 1,000 × 10⁻¹² F = 10⁻⁹ F. One microfarad is 10⁻⁶ F, so the number of microfarads is 10⁻⁹ / 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻³. The result is 0.001 µF.

An equivalent shortcut divides the picofarad number by one million. That million comes from the six powers of ten between pico and micro. In the slider, compare several pF values and watch both µF and F update. Explain the factor before trusting a decimal shift.
sections.heading: A worked conversion: pF to µF

sections.body:
Moving from a smaller unit to a larger unit produces a smaller written number. Thus 700 kHz is 700,000 Hz but only 0.7 MHz. The frequency itself remains identical. A conversion that makes all three numbers equal has ignored the prefixes.

Case matters: m is milli and M is mega. A sensible result includes its unit, and a quick conversion back should recover the original number. Use these two checks whenever an electronics answer seems a thousand or a million times too large.

lessons.title: 02 · Rearrange equations without guessing

overview.reveal: A coefficient next to a variable denotes multiplication.
anchors: Isolate a variable using an inverse operation
Test the result in the original equation
overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.outcome: Use inverse operations on both sides of an equality, then check the result by substitution.

sections.body:
The equals sign says the expression on the left has the same value as the expression on the right. A letter is a name for a quantity; it can stand for a known number or an unknown you need to find. In 4y = 2, the term 4y means four times y.

You cannot remove the 4 from one side and leave the other side untouched. Whatever operation you choose must preserve the relationship. Divide both sides by the same nonzero number to undo multiplication, or multiply both sides to undo a division.
sections.heading: Equality is a relationship to preserve

sections.body:
Start with 4y = 2. Divide both sides by 4: (4y)/4 = 2/4. The left simplifies to y because 4/4 = 1. The right is 0.5, so y = 0.5. Check in the original equation: 4 × 0.5 = 2.

That check matters. An answer of y = 8 might look like a simple multiplication, but 4 × 8 = 32 does not reproduce the original right side. The substitution test diagnoses the mistake without needing to remember an algebra shortcut.
sections.heading: Solve one small problem completely

sections.body:
In a = bc, suppose you need b. Because b is multiplied by c, divide both sides by c: a/c = bc/c = b, assuming c is nonzero. So b = a/c. If you need c instead, divide both sides by b to get c = a/b.

This same reasoning makes Ohm’s law useful. From V = IR, divide by R to get I = V/R, or divide by I to get R = V/I. The unknown tells you which form is convenient; the underlying relationship does not change.
sections.heading: Turn a product into a quotient

sections.body:
For a hypothetical V = 12 V and R = 3 kΩ, first write R = 3,000 Ω. Then I = 12/3,000 = 0.004 A. Check by multiplying: 0.004 A × 3,000 Ω = 12 V.

Use the algebra slider to change the coefficient and right-hand side. A larger coefficient with the same right side makes the unknown smaller. That directional prediction is another error check. Do not divide by zero; it changes the mathematical conditions under which the rearrangement is valid.

lessons.title: 03 · Tell a symbol from a unit

overview.reveal: R is the variable naming the quantity; kΩ describes the unit scale.
anchors: Separate a variable name from its measurement unit
Recognize common electronic and Greek notation
Resolve a symbol’s meaning from context
overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.mission: In R = 2 kΩ, what does R name?
overview.outcome: Read formulas as relationships between quantities, using the symbol and unit tables as a reference rather than a memory test.

sections.body:
In I = V/R, I names current, while amperes are the unit used to express its value. R names resistance, while Ω is its unit symbol. The source table similarly places resistance, reactance and impedance in ohms. These are different quantities even though they share a unit.

Before calculating, say what each symbol means and what unit the numerical value uses. A line such as R = 2 kΩ is a useful complete statement: it identifies the quantity, its value and its scale.
sections.heading: A letter and a unit do different jobs

sections.body:
Context decides meaning. C in Q = CV means capacitance, measured in farads. C after a charge value is the abbreviation for coulomb. For example, Q = 60 µC gives a charge, not a capacitance. Likewise, F can be the farad unit while some source notation uses capital F for frequency.

Avoid guessing from the shape of a letter. Read the local definition and the surrounding units. We use f for frequency and E for energy where defined, and keep V for voltage in the capacitor energy equation so the roles stay distinct.
sections.heading: The same character can have different meanings

sections.body:
The chapter includes a Greek-letter reference table. μ is mu and appears in the micro-prefix. Ω is uppercase omega and is used for the ohm unit. π is pi and appears in reactance and resonance formulas. You can look these up; recognizing them is more valuable here than reciting the entire alphabet.

A symbol in a formula is not automatically a measurement unit. In X_C = 1/(2πfC), π is a dimensionless numerical constant, f is frequency and C is capacitance. The result X_C has the unit ohm.
sections.heading: Greek letters are readable labels

sections.body:
A capacitor charge calculation should end in coulombs; an energy calculation should end in joules; a frequency calculation should end in hertz. If you report 60 µF for a question asking for stored charge, the unit alone reveals a category mistake.

The table also names siemens for conductance, admittance and susceptance. Recognize that unit association, but do not infer formulas for those quantities from this chapter’s table alone. A reference table is a vocabulary aid, not proof that an unseen topic has been taught.
sections.heading: Use units as a reasonableness test

lessons.title: 04 · Choose the right circuit equation

overview.reveal: Dividing V = IR by R isolates current.
anchors: Choose a useful form of Ohm’s law
Distinguish electrical power from voltage or current
overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.mission: You know V and R and want I. Which relation is direct?
overview.outcome: Calculate voltage, current, resistance and resistive power by matching the equation to the quantities you actually know.

sections.body:
Ohm’s law is V = IR. Voltage V is measured in volts, current I in amperes and resistance R in ohms. If you know any two, choose a form that isolates the third: I = V/R or R = V/I.

Read the circuit description before selecting numbers. The voltage must be across the resistor whose resistance you use. A supply label and an unrelated resistor elsewhere on a board are not automatically a valid pair. Our examples use ideal single resistive loads, so the relationship is clear.
sections.heading: Start with the quantity you need

sections.body:
For a hypothetical 12 V across 3 kΩ, write the resistance as 3,000 Ω. Substitute I = 12/3,000 = 0.004 A. Multiply by 1,000 to express this as 4 mA. Check the result: 0.004 × 3,000 = 12 V.

Predict before calculating. Increasing voltage at fixed resistance increases current; increasing resistance at fixed voltage decreases current. A result that rises when only resistance doubles needs investigation. The Ohm’s-law slider makes these two relationships visible.
sections.heading: A complete current calculation

sections.body:
Power P is measured in watts. For the resistive cases here, P = IV. With 12 V and 0.004 A, P = 0.048 W, or 48 mW. Voltage is energy per charge and current is charge per time; their product gives energy per time.

The chapter also gives P = I²R and P = V²/R. Choose the version that uses the values already known. With the same 12 V and 3,000 Ω, P = 12²/3,000 = 144/3,000 = 0.048 W. Agreement between two methods is a useful check.
sections.heading: Power describes an energy-transfer rate

sections.body:
At fixed R, power varies as V². Doubling voltage doubles current but quadruples power. At fixed current, doubling R doubles I²R power; at fixed voltage, doubling R halves V²/R power. Those different conclusions come from different quantities being held constant.

Always state what stays fixed. Use the power widget to explore this before answering a scenario. Do not interpret a calculated wattage as permission to exceed an actual component’s rating; these are idealized numerical models.
sections.heading: Why squares change the prediction

sections.body:
The saved scan review flags ambiguous prose rearrangements on p. 18. This lesson uses the accepted V = IR, P = IV, P = I²R and P = V²/R relationships. It does not treat a poorly delimited radical in the source as a new rule.

Work in this order: name the unknown, list known quantities and units, convert prefixes, select an equation, substitute with units, calculate, then check direction and scale. The sequence is more dependable than hunting through a formula wheel without understanding what its letters mean.

lessons.title: 05 · Combine resistor paths

overview.reveal: Series total resistance is the sum of individual resistances.
anchors: Add resistances in one series path
Use reciprocal addition for parallel paths
Apply magnitude checks to catch network mistakes
overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.mission: Two resistors share one series path. What combines directly?
overview.outcome: Identify series versus parallel before choosing the arithmetic, and test the result against physical path reasoning.

sections.body:
Series resistors lie in one path, so their resistances add. If the values are 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ, the total is 3 kΩ. Parallel resistors provide separate paths between the same two nodes. Their equivalent resistance is found by adding reciprocal resistances and taking the reciprocal of that sum.

The circuit arrangement chooses the rule. The fact that a page lists several resistor values does not tell you whether to add them directly. First identify how the paths connect.
sections.heading: One path or several branches?

sections.body:
For 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω, start with 1/R_T = 1/6 + 1/3. Use a common denominator: 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2. That sum has units of inverse ohms. Take its reciprocal to obtain R_T = 2 Ω.

For two positive resistors, you can also use R_T = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Here 6 × 3/(6 + 3) = 18/9 = 2 Ω. The shortcut is for two branches, not a rule to multiply every resistor in a larger network.
sections.heading: Work a parallel example slowly

sections.body:
For n equal resistors of resistance R, the parallel total is R/n. Three 1 kΩ branches therefore have an equivalent of 1,000/3 ≈ 333.3 Ω. At an ideal 5 V, each branch carries 5 mA and the total is 15 mA. The same total follows from 5/333.3 ≈ 0.015 A.

R/n assumes equal values. If the branches are unequal, use the reciprocal rule rather than averaging their resistances or dividing an arbitrary branch by the number of branches.
sections.heading: Equal branches provide a useful shortcut

sections.body:
A positive series total is larger than any of its individual resistors. A parallel equivalent with at least two positive finite branches is smaller than the smallest branch. The 2 Ω result for 6 Ω and 3 Ω passes that check; 9 Ω would not.

In the widget, hold R₂ fixed and increase R₁. The parallel equivalent increases because that branch provides less conductance, but it stays below R₂. Adding another positive parallel branch reduces the total resistance. These checks often find a wrong formula faster than repeating the arithmetic.

lessons.title: 06 · Explain a battery’s voltage sag

overview.reveal: The load current passes through both external and internal resistance.
anchors: Include internal resistance in the current path
Explain why loaded terminal voltage is below EMF
overview.caution: Virtual battery models do not authorize shorting or testing a real battery. Actual source, fuse and component ratings are not supplied here.
overview.mission: Where does internal resistance sit in this battery model?
overview.outcome: Distinguish internal EMF from loaded terminal voltage with a simple series-resistance model.

sections.body:
EMF is the source voltage in the battery model. Internal resistance r is placed in series with the external load R. The current must pass through both, so the total resistance is R + r.

That makes I = EMF/(R + r). Do not use only R unless you are intentionally using an ideal source model with negligible internal resistance. The two models answer different questions; neither lets you infer a real battery’s internal resistance from its label alone.
sections.heading: The model has two resistances

sections.body:
Let EMF = 6 V, the load be 5 Ω, and internal resistance be 1 Ω. Total resistance is 6 Ω, giving I = 6/6 = 1 A. The internal drop is Ir = 1 × 1 = 1 V. The voltage across the load is IR = 1 × 5 = 5 V.

The voltages add: 1 V inside the model plus 5 V at its terminals equals the 6 V EMF. You can also obtain terminal voltage as EMF − Ir. Using both routes checks that the same current and resistances were used consistently.
sections.heading: Work a complete hypothetical example

sections.body:
Terminal voltage is the voltage available across the external load. For positive internal resistance and nonzero load current, it is less than EMF. If the load resistance becomes very large, current becomes small and the internal drop becomes small.

Decrease the load resistance in the widget. The current increases, so the internal voltage drop grows. Terminal voltage falls even though the model’s EMF setting has not changed. This is a model of load-dependent sag, not a command to short or heavily load a real battery.
sections.heading: Connect the numbers to sag

sections.body:
The saved source example gives I = 1.5 V/6.25 Ω = 0.24 A, or 240 mA. That denominator includes the external and internal series resistances. Our 6 V example uses different explicitly hypothetical values to make the separate drops easy to see.

Always identify whether a voltage is EMF or terminal voltage. Reporting the 6 V setting as a measured loaded terminal voltage in our example would ignore the 1 V internal drop. A calculation does not establish safe real-battery ratings or a test method.

lessons.title: 07 · Read a sine wave’s amplitudes

overview.reveal: Peak-to-peak is maximum minus minimum: 10 − (−10) = 20 V.
anchors: Locate a sine wave’s positive and negative extrema
Apply RMS conversion only to a sine wave
overview.caution: All waveforms here are idealized. The chapter’s higher-voltage examples are paper exercises, not instructions to probe live equipment.
overview.mission: A centered sine wave runs from +10 V to −10 V. Its peak-to-peak value is…
overview.outcome: Separate signed instantaneous voltage from peak, peak-to-peak and sinusoidal RMS values.

sections.body:
A sine wave goes through a repeating cycle. The source figure shows 0° through 360°, with a positive extreme at 90° and a negative extreme at 270°. A negative instantaneous voltage is a signed value relative to the chosen reference; it is not a negative amplitude magnitude.

If a centered sine wave reaches +10 V and −10 V, its peak magnitude is 10 V. The distance from its lowest to highest voltage is 20 V, which is its peak-to-peak value.
sections.heading: One cycle includes both polarities

sections.body:
For the centered sine wave in this lesson, V_pp = 2V_p. A 6 V peak corresponds to 12 V peak-to-peak. Going the other direction divides by two: a 24 V peak-to-peak sine wave has a 12 V peak.

Read the amplitude label before entering a number into another equation. Calling a 20 V peak-to-peak value a 20 V peak value makes the assumed amplitude twice too large. The waveform widget shows the positive and negative extremes together.
sections.heading: Peak and peak-to-peak answer different questions

sections.body:
For an ideal sinusoid, V_rms = V_p/√2, approximately 0.707V_p. Conversely, V_p = √2V_rms, approximately 1.414V_rms. A 10 V peak sine wave therefore has approximately 7.07 V RMS. Its peak-to-peak value remains 20 V.

RMS is a different amplitude measure with an equivalent heating interpretation for a resistor under appropriate conditions. The sine-wave conversion factor is not a universal rule for a square wave, pulse train or arbitrary signal.
sections.heading: What the RMS conversion means here

sections.body:
The chapter supplies rounded factors 0.707, 1.414 and 2.828. Their products may not return exactly one because they are rounded. Keep adequate precision until the final answer and use an approximation sign when applying these factors.

Start from a known labeled measure, choose the corresponding conversion, then check order: for a nonzero centered sine wave, RMS magnitude is below peak magnitude, and peak-to-peak is twice peak. Source examples with high voltages are paper calculations, not practical measurement instructions.

lessons.title: 08 · Move between period and frequency

anchors: Separate cycles per second from seconds per cycle
Convert ms and kHz before using a reciprocal
overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.outcome: Use reciprocal relationships and unit conversions to describe how often a waveform repeats and how long one cycle lasts.

sections.body:
Frequency f counts cycles per second and is measured in hertz. Period T is the time required for one complete cycle and is measured in seconds. A 100 Hz waveform repeats 100 times each second; each cycle therefore occupies 1/100 second.

The relationships are T = 1/f and f = 1/T. They are reciprocals, not equal numerical quantities. A higher frequency corresponds to a shorter period because more cycles must fit into the same second.
sections.heading: Two views of one repeating signal

sections.body:
For a hypothetical period of 2 ms, first convert: 2 ms = 0.002 s. Then f = 1/0.002 = 500 Hz. Check by multiplying: 500 cycles/s × 0.002 s/cycle = 1.

Entering 2 into a seconds-based formula would describe a 2-second period and give 0.5 Hz. The missing milli-prefix causes a thousandfold frequency error. Read the time unit before touching the reciprocal key.
sections.heading: Work from milliseconds to hertz

sections.body:
A frequency of 2 kHz is 2,000 Hz. Period is 1/2,000 = 0.0005 s, or 0.5 ms. A useful compatible-unit relation is T in ms = 1/f in kHz, but understand why it works before using it as a shortcut.

In the widget, raise frequency from 1,000 to 2,000 Hz. The period falls from 1 ms to 0.5 ms. Doubling either quantity halves its reciprocal; it does not make both larger.
sections.heading: Work from kilohertz to period

sections.body:
The saved extraction flags the chapter’s display of 1/60 s as 16.6 ms without an approximation sign. The exact reciprocal is a repeating decimal; ordinary rounding to the nearest tenth of a millisecond gives 16.7 ms.

This lesson identifies 16.6 ms as the source’s approximate displayed value rather than claiming exact equality or nearest-tenth rounding. Keep calculator precision until the last step and label your rounded result appropriately.

overview.reveal: Charge is directly proportional to capacitance and voltage.
anchors: Use Q = CV with capacitance in farads

overview.caution: Stored-energy examples and sliders do not authorize charging or handling physical capacitors. Real stored charge can create hazards.
overview.outcome: Calculate stored charge and stored energy, then predict why voltage changes affect them differently.

sections.body:
Capacitance C is measured in farads. Charge Q is measured in coulombs and follows Q = CV. Stored energy E is measured in joules and follows E = 0.5CV² in the accepted capacitor model.

Charge and energy are related, but they are not interchangeable. One says how much charge is associated with the voltage and capacitance; the other measures stored energy. Write the desired quantity and its unit before choosing a formula.
sections.heading: Two quantities are stored, with different units

sections.body:
The source uses C = 5 µF and V = 12 V. Convert capacitance: 5 µF = 5 × 10⁻⁶ F. Then Q = (5 × 10⁻⁶)(12) = 60 × 10⁻⁶ C = 60 µC.

The final C is the coulomb unit, not the capacitance variable. The multiplication uses capacitance in farads and voltage in volts. A result of 60 C would ignore the micro-prefix and be one million times too large.
sections.heading: Work the charge example from the extraction

sections.body:
Using the clear accepted energy formula with those same values gives E = 0.5 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 12². Square voltage first: 12² = 144. Half of 5 × 144 is 360, so E = 360 × 10⁻⁶ J = 360 µJ.

This is an independently shown teaching calculation from the accepted formula. The extraction flags conflicting right-column source notation that reuses E ambiguously; that expression is not presented as a reliable additional rule.
sections.heading: Calculate energy independently

sections.body:
At fixed capacitance, doubling voltage doubles Q = CV but quadruples E = 0.5CV². At fixed voltage, doubling capacitance doubles both. The energy widget displays both quantities so you can compare those effects without confusing their units.

In the default 100 µF, 5 V example, charge is 500 µC and energy is 1,250 µJ. Increasing voltage to 10 V produces 1,000 µC and 5,000 µJ. These are virtual calculations, not instructions to charge a real capacitor.

sections.body:
The accepted chapter relationships give direct addition for parallel capacitance: C_T = C₁ + C₂ + …. Series capacitance uses reciprocal addition: 1/C_T = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ….

Do not transfer the resistor rule solely because the words series and parallel look familiar. The relevant component quantity is different. Decide the component type and its arrangement before selecting a formula.
sections.heading: Capacitors combine differently from resistors

sections.body:
Two 10 µF capacitors in parallel give C_T = 10 + 10 = 20 µF. Keep all values in the same unit while adding. If one value is given in nF and another in µF, convert one before adding their numbers.

The source material spans pp. 20–21. The saved extraction supports the numerical examples across those pages but does not justify assigning each example to one precise page, so the attribution remains collective.
sections.heading: A parallel example

sections.body:
Three equal 10 µF capacitors in series give C_T = C/n = 10/3 µF ≈ 3.33 µF. For two unequal capacitors, product-over-sum is convenient: C_T = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). For 10 µF and 20 µF, this gives 200/30 ≈ 6.67 µF.

The shortcut is limited to two series capacitors. For a larger set, add all reciprocals and invert the resulting sum. Rounding too early can spoil the final reciprocal.
sections.heading: A series example

sections.body:
For at least two positive finite capacitances in series, the equivalent is below the smallest individual capacitance. In parallel, the total exceeds each individual value. Thus the 6.67 µF series result is sensible for 10 and 20 µF, while 30 µF would describe their parallel total.

Use the widget to change one capacitance and compare both arrangements. The total responds continuously, but the series and parallel outputs follow different rules. These are idealized capacitances, without claims about a physical capacitor’s voltage rating or stored-energy safety.

overview.reveal: Multiply resistance in ohms by capacitance in farads to obtain seconds.
anchors: Calculate τ = RC with compatible units

overview.caution: The source’s 100 V values are paper examples. No high-voltage construction, discharge method or handling procedure is authorized here.
overview.mission: What is the RC time constant?
overview.outcome: Calculate RC timing and read ideal exponential behavior without mistaking an approximation for exact completion.

sections.body:
The RC time constant is τ = RC, with resistance in ohms and capacitance in farads. Its unit is second. τ tells you the characteristic pace of the change; it is not a fixed stopwatch time at which every change suddenly stops.

At fixed C, larger R gives a larger time constant. At fixed R, larger C also gives a larger time constant. Doubling both therefore multiplies τ by four, which you can test with the two sliders.
sections.heading: Resistance and capacitance set the timescale

sections.body:
For R = 10 kΩ and C = 5 µF, convert R to 10,000 Ω and C to 5 × 10⁻⁶ F. Then τ = 10,000 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.05 s, or 50 ms.

A compatible shortcut multiplies kΩ by µF to get milliseconds: 10 × 5 = 50 ms. The shortcut works because 10³ × 10⁻⁶ = 10⁻³. Keep that factor visible so you do not mistakenly label 50 as seconds.
sections.heading: Calculate the chapter’s accepted example

sections.body:
The accepted source example gives 63.2 V after one charging time constant for a 100 V final level. That is approximately 63.2% of the final level, leaving approximately 36.8% of the difference still to close. It does not mean the capacitor is fully charged.

Our ideal charging graph uses the teaching model fraction = 1 − exp(−t/τ) to represent the exponential behavior. At t = τ, it gives about 0.632. The graph is a calculated model, not a reproduction of the disputed printed labels.
sections.heading: Understand the one-τ charging point

sections.body:
In the ideal charging model, five time constants gives approximately 99.3% of the final level. The remaining difference is small but not zero. The response approaches the final level asymptotically rather than becoming mathematically complete at a finite time.

The saved extraction flags an incorrect-looking discharge percentage, a repeated final time label and an unqualified completion claim in the source figure. Those labels are not adopted here. Use the accepted τ calculation and the explicitly identified ideal charging model instead.
sections.heading: Five time constants is close, not exact

sections.body:
If τ increases, reaching the same fraction of the final value takes longer. At a fixed elapsed time, the slower charging response has reached a smaller fraction. The widget rescales its time axis with τ, so check the milliseconds shown on that axis rather than comparing curve shapes alone.

The shape in normalized time remains the same. This separates a response’s exponential shape from its real time duration, and explains why two RC circuits can share the same percentage-at-one-τ rule while changing at different speeds.

overview.reveal: The entire frequency-capacitance product is in the denominator.
anchors: Predict inverse changes with frequency or capacitance

overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.mission: What is the accepted capacitive-reactance formula?
overview.outcome: Calculate a capacitor’s ideal AC reactance and distinguish its magnitude from its phase relationship.

sections.body:
The capacitor’s ideal capacitive reactance magnitude is X_C = 1/(2πfC), measured in ohms. f is frequency in hertz, C is capacitance in farads, and π is the numerical constant pi.

Although X_C shares the ohm unit with resistance, a reactive element’s AC behavior includes phase. Do not treat a reactance label as a statement that the component behaves like an ordinary resistor in every respect.
sections.heading: Reactance is not a resistor value

sections.body:
For a hypothetical f = 1 kHz and C = 1 µF, convert to 1,000 Hz and 1 × 10⁻⁶ F. The denominator is 2π × 1,000 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 0.006283. Now take its reciprocal: X_C ≈ 159.15 Ω.

Stopping at 0.006283 would report the denominator rather than reactance. Enter the entire product inside the denominator, and retain enough precision until the final reciprocal. A calculator’s grouping matters.
sections.heading: Work through the reciprocal

sections.body:
Frequency and capacitance both appear in the denominator. Doubling either while holding the other fixed halves X_C. Doubling both reduces it to a quarter of its original value.

The widget uses frequency in kHz and capacitance in nF, with those prefixes converted internally. Read its units before copying a number. Increase frequency at a fixed capacitance and observe the falling reactance curve; then change capacitance and see the curve shift.
sections.heading: Predict before moving a control

sections.body:
The accepted source figure shows capacitor current leading voltage by 90°. A phase lead describes the relative position of repeating waveforms, not a larger amplitude or a physical instruction about which wire carries current first.

The figure’s current phasor points right and voltage phasor points down under its chosen reference convention. A downward phasor is not a claim that instantaneous voltage is always negative. Keep phase-reference orientation, instantaneous sign and amplitude as separate ideas.

overview.reveal: Inductive reactance uses a direct frequency-inductance product.

overview.caution: These are paper calculations and idealized simulations, not instructions to build or energize a circuit.
overview.mission: Which equation gives ideal inductive reactance magnitude?
overview.outcome: Calculate inductive reactance and predict why its frequency trend is opposite to capacitive reactance.

sections.body:
The accepted relationship is X_L = 2πfL. X_L is inductive reactance magnitude in ohms, f is frequency in hertz and L is inductance in henrys. Unlike the capacitor equation, the frequency-inductance product is not inside a reciprocal.

This difference determines the trend: higher frequency gives larger inductive reactance, while higher frequency gives smaller capacitive reactance at fixed capacitance.
sections.heading: Read the inductive-reactance equation

sections.body:
For hypothetical f = 1 kHz and L = 10 mH, use 1,000 Hz and 0.01 H. Then X_L = 2π × 1,000 × 0.01 = 20π Ω ≈ 62.83 Ω.

The prefixes cancel numerically when multiplying kHz by mH, because 10³ × 10⁻³ = 1. That does not mean prefixes can always be ignored; it means this particular compatible product has a net scale factor of one. State that reason if you use the shortcut.
sections.heading: Work a complete numerical example

sections.body:
Doubling frequency at fixed L doubles X_L. Doubling L at fixed frequency also doubles X_L. Doubling both multiplies reactance by four. Compare those predictions with the rising widget curve.

For a capacitor, doubling frequency halves X_C instead. The two trends matter when both components appear in a series circuit. Do not subtract their values before checking that they describe the same frequency and are expressed in compatible units.
sections.heading: Predict proportional changes

sections.body:
The source extraction establishes that voltage leads current in its inductive-reactance discussion. It does not supply a numerical inductive phase angle as accepted evidence, so this lesson keeps the relationship qualitative rather than adding a source-attributed angle.

A statement about which waveform leads does not tell you the total phase of a circuit containing resistance and other reactances. A component’s reactance magnitude, a component phase relationship and complete-circuit impedance are related but separate ideas.

sections.body:
For this series model, define X_net = X_L − X_C. A positive difference is inductive and a negative one is capacitive. The magnitude relationship is |Z| = √(R² + X_net²).

The printed source example writes the difference in the opposite order before squaring. Either order gives the same magnitude because the square removes the sign, but it does not mean the sign is irrelevant to interpreting predominance. We state our convention explicitly.
sections.heading: Define the reactive difference before squaring

sections.body:
The source gives R = 3 Ω, X_L = 16 Ω and X_C = 20 Ω. Our signed difference is 16 − 20 = −4 Ω, so the circuit is predominantly capacitive. The magnitude is √(3² + (−4)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 Ω.

Do not add 3 + 16 + 20 to obtain 39 Ω. Reactive contributions oppose one another here, and resistance combines with the net reactive contribution through the magnitude relation rather than direct arithmetic addition.
sections.heading: Work the accepted 3–4–5 example

sections.body:
A magnitude cannot be negative. A net reactance of −4 Ω and one of +4 Ω at the same R give the same numerical magnitude, but different predominance. If X_L = X_C, the net reactive difference is zero and the magnitude equals R in this ideal series model.

The accepted source phasor sketch labels its example capacitive. We do not add an unsupported total circuit phase angle or use the magnitude formula to claim the current is leading by a particular numerical angle.
sections.heading: The square does not make the physical interpretation disappear

sections.body:
The simulator takes frequency, L, C and R, then calculates X_L, X_C and |Z|. It is not asking you to enter reactance values into an inductance or capacitance field. Watch the units and distinguish the inputs from the derived outputs.

With frequency, L and R fixed, increasing C lowers X_C. The complete impedance may decrease toward cancellation and then increase beyond it; do not claim that every capacitance increase always lowers |Z|. Compare the changing difference, not just one component in isolation.

sections.body:
The accepted chapter relationship sets X_L = X_C. Substituting their formulas gives 2πfL = 1/(2πfC). Solving that relation gives f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)), with L in henrys, C in farads and frequency in hertz.

This lesson uses the source’s explicitly series example and the ideal model. It does not adopt the source’s ambiguous maximum-current wording as a general statement about every series and parallel resonant circuit.
sections.heading: Resonance starts with a matching condition

sections.body:
The source example uses 200 µH and 200 pF. Convert them independently: 200 µH = 2 × 10⁻⁴ H and 200 pF = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ F. Their product is 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ H·F.

Taking the square root gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ s. The exponent is halved under the square root; the leading 4 becomes 2. Confusing pico with micro changes the capacitance by a millionfold factor, and the square root turns that into a thousandfold frequency error.
sections.heading: Keep both prefixes visible

sections.body:
The denominator is 2π × 2 × 10⁻⁷ s ≈ 1.256637 × 10⁻⁶ s. Its reciprocal is approximately 795,775 Hz, or 795.8 kHz. The source reports approximately 795 kHz; we distinguish that display from our more precise independent recalculation.

Keep the whole LC product inside the square root, and the whole 2π√(LC) product inside the reciprocal. Leaving out either the square root or reciprocal produces a very different kind of calculation.
sections.heading: Finish the calculation before rounding

sections.body:
At about 795.8 kHz with those component values, X_L = 2πfL is about 1,000 Ω. Calculating X_C = 1/(2πfC) gives about the same 1,000 Ω. Agreement checks the resonance calculation using the underlying condition.

In the ideal series RLC model, cancellation of equal reactance magnitudes leaves the resistance in the impedance magnitude. It does not imply every real resonant circuit has zero impedance, or that component tolerances and losses disappear.
sections.heading: Check the condition using a second route

sections.body:
Because frequency is inversely proportional to √(LC), quadrupling C while holding L fixed halves f_r. Doubling C reduces f_r by a factor of √2, not by a factor of two. The same statements apply to changing L while holding C fixed.

Use the resonance widget to test the difference between a twofold and fourfold change. Read the component units before comparing examples. The goal is to combine prefix handling, square roots, reciprocals and a physical condition into one dependable chain of reasoning.

sections.body:
Read prefixes before calculating: milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶ and pico = 10⁻¹². For example, 1,000 pF = 0.001 µF.
Rearrange an equality by applying the same inverse operation to both sides. Check the result in the original equation.
Keep the quantity symbol separate from its unit: resistance, reactance and impedance use Ω; frequency uses Hz, capacitance F and inductance H.
Choose the relationship that fits the known values: I = V/R and P = VI = I²R = V²/R. At fixed R, doubling V doubles I and quadruples P.
Resistors add in series; in parallel their reciprocals add. With positive branch resistances, the parallel equivalent is below either branch.
Internal resistance causes source voltage sag under load: I = EMF/(Rload + r), and terminal voltage = EMF − Ir.
For an ideal sine wave, peak-to-peak = 2 × peak and RMS = peak/√2. Do not apply the sine-wave RMS conversion to every waveform.
Period and frequency are reciprocals: T = 1/f. Higher frequency means a shorter cycle, not a larger amplitude.
Capacitor charge and energy are different: Q = CV and E = ½CV². At fixed C, doubling V doubles charge but quadruples energy.
Capacitors add in parallel and use reciprocal sums in series—the opposite combination rule to resistors.
The RC time constant is τ = RC. Ideal charging reaches about 63.2% after one τ; the final value is approached rather than reached exactly.
Capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC): increasing f or C lowers it. In the ideal capacitor, current leads voltage.
Simple inductor combination rules require negligible mutual coupling: series adds; parallel uses reciprocal sums.
Inductive reactance is X_L = 2πfL: increasing f or L raises it. The accepted source describes voltage leading current.
For the ideal series RLC model, |Z| = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²). Preserve the signed difference when identifying inductive or capacitive predominance.
Ideal resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, with f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)). Convert prefixes first and check the result using both reactances.

units.goal: Express quantities using powers of ten and convert electronic values between metric prefixes without changing their physical magnitude.
units.focus: Practice scientific notation and conversions such as pF to µF and kHz to Hz or MHz. Use intermediate powers-of-ten steps, prefix capitalization and magnitude checks rather than memorized decimal shifts alone.
units.title: Scientific Notation and Electronic Prefix Conversions

units.goal: Solve simple equations and isolate a desired variable while preserving equality.
units.focus: Use a = bc and 4y = 2 to explain inverse operations and substitution checks. Supply brief arithmetic support within practice as needed rather than inventing a separate source lesson on unseen mathematics.
units.title: Variables, Equality and Formula Rearrangement

units.goal: Distinguish a formula variable from a unit abbreviation and interpret the chapter’s electronic and Greek notation.
units.focus: Use the units and Greek-letter tables as reference tools. Distinguish resistance, reactance and impedance from their shared ohm unit; recognize siemens entries without expanding into unseen admittance theory. Define context-dependent symbols locally, including capacitance versus coulombs and voltage versus energy notation.
units.title: Reading Formula Symbols and Units

units.goal: Select and apply a verified voltage, current, resistance or power relation from the known quantities.
units.focus: Reinforce V = IR, its quotient forms, P = IV, P = I²R and P = V²/R with mixed known-and-unknown problems. Compare the memory aids with explicit algebra and check units. Do not use the extraction’s disputed power-law prose or extend resistive power expressions indiscriminately to reactive AC loads.
units.title: Ohm’s Law and Power Calculation Practice

units.goal: Calculate series and parallel resistance totals and judge whether the result is plausible.
units.focus: Add series resistances, evaluate reciprocal sums for parallel resistances and use R/n for equal parallel resistors. Provide written calculation practice that complements the existing virtual laboratory rather than repeating its measurement approach.
units.title: Resistor Network Totals

units.goal: Explain why battery terminal voltage falls under load and calculate current using external plus internal resistance.
units.focus: Interpret internal resistance as part of the series circuit and connect load current to internal voltage drop. Work through the verified 1.5 V and 6.25 Ω total-resistance example, then distinguish EMF from loaded terminal voltage.
units.title: Battery EMF, Internal Resistance and Terminal Voltage

units.goal: Read a sinusoidal cycle and distinguish peak, peak-to-peak and RMS voltage.
units.focus: Locate the positive and negative extrema within a 0°–360° cycle and connect each amplitude measure to the diagram. Apply the source’s rounded conversion factors only to sine waves, with practice identifying the requested measure before calculating.
units.title: Sinusoidal Waveforms and Amplitude Measures

units.goal: Convert between period and frequency with correct seconds, hertz and metric prefixes.
units.focus: Use T = 1/f and f = 1/T with explicit reciprocal entry and unit conversion. Check that increasing frequency decreases period, and treat the source’s 16.6 ms display for 60 Hz as rounded rather than exact.
units.title: Period and Frequency Calculations

units.goal: Relate capacitance and voltage to stored charge and electric-field energy.
units.focus: Introduce farads, coulombs and joules, then apply Q = CV and the clear energy definition E = 0.5CV². Compare linear voltage dependence of charge with squared voltage dependence of energy. Use the verified charge example and avoid the unresolved notation in the source’s energy solution.
units.title: Capacitor Charge and Stored Energy

units.goal: Calculate equivalent capacitance for series and parallel combinations.
units.focus: Practice additive parallel totals, reciprocal series totals, the two-capacitor product-over-sum expression and C/n for equal series capacitors. Contrast the operations with resistor totals and check results against the individual values.
units.title: Capacitor Network Totals

units.goal: Calculate an RC time constant and explain its role in exponential capacitor charging and discharging.
units.focus: Use TC = RC with ohms and farads, reproduce the 0.05 s example and interpret the verified 63.2 V charging value after one time constant with 100 V applied. Keep the exercise mathematical; exclude disputed discharge labels and unqualified claims of exact completion after five time constants.
units.title: RC Time Constants and Exponential Response

units.goal: Explain capacitive opposition to AC and relate frequency, capacitance and the current-leading phase relationship.
units.focus: Apply X_C = 1/(2πfC), interpret reactance in ohms and compare how frequency or capacitance changes its magnitude. Read the source’s 90° current-leading waveform and phasor views without introducing advanced phasor algebra.
units.title: Capacitive Reactance and Phase

units.goal: Explain inductance as opposition to changing current and identify the limits of simple inductor-combination rules.
units.focus: Introduce henrys, practice the source’s simple series and parallel examples, and distinguish reinforcing from opposing magnetic-field relationships. Flag mutual inductance as a qualification; do not infer a general coupled-inductor parallel rule from the incomplete prose.
units.title: Inductance and Combining Inductors

units.goal: Calculate inductive reactance and explain the voltage-leading phase relationship.
units.focus: Apply X_L = 2πfL with correct henry and hertz conversions. Compare its increasing frequency dependence and voltage-leading behavior with the capacitive case, keeping calculations distinct from qualitative phase interpretation.
units.title: Inductive Reactance and Phase

units.goal: Combine resistance and opposing reactances to find series-RLC impedance magnitude and identify capacitive or inductive predominance.
units.focus: Interpret the reactive difference before applying Z = √((X_C − X_L)² + R²). Reproduce the 3 Ω, 16 Ω and 20 Ω example yielding 5 Ω, distinguishing positive impedance magnitude from the direction of reactive predominance. Do not generalize the ambiguous parallel formula to arbitrary networks.
units.title: Series-RLC Impedance and Phasor Interpretation

units.goal: Explain resonance through equal inductive and capacitive reactances and calculate resonant frequency.
units.focus: Connect X_C = X_L to f_r = 1/(2π√(LC)) and work through the 200 µH, 200 pF example giving approximately 795 kHz. Use prefix, square-root and dimensional checks; retain the explicitly series context and avoid unsupported parallel-resonance current claims.
units.title: Resonance and Resonant Frequency

chapter_outline.rationale: The outline separates distinct calculation skills from new circuit concepts rather than targeting a lesson count. Prefixes, algebra, Ohm’s law, power and resistor combinations reinforce existing lessons and therefore go to review; the remaining objectives introduce source-supported material. Pure calculation units are independent and have no completion prerequisites. Conceptual gates are used only where understanding reactive behavior is necessary for impedance or resonance. Each unit should include defined symbols, a verified worked example where available, unit checks and clearly labeled newly authored practice. Unresolved source equations, cropped text, questionable RC graph labels and unsupported coupling or parallel-resonance generalizations are excluded. Source high-voltage examples remain paper calculations, not laboratory instructions.
